cards.title: A small-town tinkerer
cards.body: Claude Shannon was born in 1916 and grew up in Gaylord, a small town in northern Michigan. He built model planes and a radio-controlled boat, and fixed the town's broken radios. His hero was Thomas Edison, who later turned out to be a distant relative.

visual.caption: Where he grew up, what he built and mended, and who he looked up to

cards.title: A fence telegraph
cards.body: As a boy he turned a half-mile stretch of barbed-wire fence into a private telegraph line to a friend's house, powered by batteries. His favorite story was Poe's "The Gold-Bug", which ends with someone cracking a secret cipher.

steps: Half a mile of barbed wire
visual.caption: Coded taps on one key travelled along the fence wire to the other

cards.title: College years
cards.body: At Michigan he earned two degrees at once: mathematics and electrical engineering.

cards.title: Boole's algebra
cards.body: In the 1800s George Boole wrote logic as algebra: true is 1, false is 0, and statements combine with AND, OR and NOT. Shannon first met it in a philosophy class at Michigan, where it was taught as a curiosity with no practical use.

visual.caption: AND needs both to be 1; OR needs at least one

cards.title: Series is AND
cards.body: A closed switch is 1 and an open switch is 0. Put two switches in series, one after the other, and current flows only if both are closed.

frames.caption: a = 0, b = 0: a gap in the line, so no current: the lamp is off
a = 0, b = 1: a gap in the line, so no current: the lamp is off
a = 1, b = 0: a gap in the line, so no current: the lamp is off
a = 1, b = 1: both closed, so current flows: the lamp is on

cards.title: Parallel is OR
cards.body: In parallel, side by side, current flows if either switch, or both, is closed. That is OR, so 1 + 1 = 1. A contact that opens when its relay fires acts as NOT.

visual.caption: The same truth table, now read as circuits. Last row: 1 + 1 = 1

cards.title: In Python
cards.code:
def series(a, b):    # AND
    return a and b

def parallel(a, b):  # OR
    return a or b

print(series(1, 0))    # 0
print(parallel(1, 0))  # 1
print(parallel(1, 1))  # 1

cards.title: Simplify on paper
cards.body: A circuit is now an equation, so shrink it with algebra before touching a wire: y·z + y·z' = y·(z + z'). A switch is closed or open, so z + z' is always 1, leaving just y: one switch does the work of four contacts. Also handy: y·y = y and y + y = y.

visual.caption: The last two columns match in every row, so the circuit equals plain y

cards.title: The 1937 thesis
cards.body: The thesis was "A Symbolic Analysis of Relay and Switching Circuits". It turned circuit design from guesswork into a science, and every digital computer's logic gates follow the same idea.

events.what: George Boole writes logic as algebra

It is published, and wins the Alfred Noble Prize

cards.title: Into Bell Labs
cards.body: His PhD applied algebra to genetics. At Bell Labs he checked the math for SIGSALY, a secret phone scrambler, without being told what it was for.

cards.title: The one-time pad
cards.body: A one-time pad hides a message with a key that meets four rules. In a classified 1945 report, "A Mathematical Theory of Cryptography", Shannon gave the first proof that such a cipher cannot be broken, even with unlimited computing power.

visual.caption: The key must pass all four rules, or the proof no longer holds

cards.title: XOR as a pad
cards.body: XOR (^) flips the message bits wherever the key has a 1. Doing it again with the same key flips them back, because k ^ k = 0. Time O(n) and space O(n) for n bits.
cards.code:
msg = 0b1100
key = 0b1010
c = msg ^ key
print(bin(c))        # 0b110
print(bin(c ^ key))  # 0b1100

frames.caption: The message: 1100
The key: 1010. Its 1s mark the bits that will flip
msg ^ key = 0110 (Python prints 0b110): marked bits flipped
XOR the key again: 1100, the message is back

cards.title: Tea with Turing
cards.body: In 1942 Alan Turing came to the US to inspect secret speech-scrambling work. He and Shannon met over tea in the Bell Labs cafeteria.

cards.title: The 1948 paper
cards.body: The paper was "A Mathematical Theory of Communication". To Shannon, communication meant getting a copy of a chosen message to the far end. What the message means does not matter to that engineering job.

events.what: Nyquist, a Bell engineer: information is about choice
Hartley, also at Bell, sees the same
Shannon's paper, in two parts, Bell System Technical Journal
Book version adds an essay by Warren Weaver

visual.caption: Two Bell engineers pointed the way; Shannon's paper finished the job

cards.title: Six boxes, one path
cards.body: Shannon drew every link as the same boxes. A sixth box, the noise source, feeds into the channel and corrupts the signal.

visual.caption: Five boxes in a row; the sixth, the noise source, attacks the channel

cards.title: Information is choice
cards.body: Earlier Bell engineers, Nyquist (1924) and Hartley (1927), saw that information is about choice: what counts is how many messages you could have sent, not which one you did.

visual.caption: The same message carries more when it was picked from more possibilities

cards.title: One bit
cards.body: A bit is the information in picking one of two outcomes that are equally likely, like a fair coin. John Tukey, a colleague, suggested the name at lunch. Each extra bit doubles the options, so n equally likely options take log2(n) bits.

frames.caption: 1 bit: 2 options, and log2(2) = 1
2 bits: 4 options, and log2(4) = 2
3 bits: 8 options, and log2(8) = 3

cards.title: Measuring surprise
cards.body: Information is uncertainty that gets cleared up. If you already know the result, you learn nothing: a coin with heads on both sides gives 0 bits per flip. An outcome with probability p carries log2(1/p) bits of surprise.

visual.caption: The rarer the outcome, the bigger the surprise; a sure thing gives none

cards.title: The formula
cards.body: Entropy H is the average surprise: add up p · log2(1/p) over all outcomes. It is largest when all outcomes are equally likely; then n outcomes give log2(n) bits. The more lopsided the odds, the lower H.

visual.caption: Equal odds reach log2(n): 1 bit for 2, 3 bits for 8. Lopsided coins fall below

cards.title: A worked example
cards.body: A coin that lands heads 80% of the time. Work out each outcome's surprise, weight it by its probability, and add.

frames.caption: Start with the two outcomes and their probabilities
Surprise: the common heads barely surprises, the rare tails does
Weight each surprise by how often it happens
Add the last column: H = 0.72 bits, less than a fair coin's 1

cards.title: In Python
cards.body: Time O(k) for k outcomes, O(1) extra space.

cards.title: Lopsided coins
cards.body: A coin that lands heads 90% of the time gives about 0.47 bits per flip; at 99% it drops to about 0.08. Shannon's paper showed this curve.

visual.caption: The peak is 1 bit at 50/50; the curve falls to 0 at either extreme

cards.title: Why "entropy"?
cards.body: The name borrows from physics, where entropy measures disorder.

visual.caption: A good story about the name, and why not to trust it

sources.title: A Mind at Play (Soni & Goodman, 2017), ch. 16

cards.title: The predictable part
cards.body: Redundancy is the part of a message you could have guessed from the rest. Shannon estimated English is about half redundant, and later put it as high as 80%. It is also why codebreakers can crack ciphers: letter patterns leak through.

visual.caption: "Thank y_u": the missing letter is no mystery, so it carried no news

cards.title: Short codes, common symbols
cards.body: To compress, give frequent symbols short codewords and rare ones long codewords. The average length is the sum of p × (codeword length).

visual.caption: The most common symbol, w, gets 1 bit; the rarest get 3

cards.title: Only one way to split
cards.body: Use a prefix code: no codeword is the start of another, so a stream of bits splits up only one way.

frames.caption: Nine bits arrive with no gaps between codewords
10 is a codeword and starts no other: x. So far: x
0 is a codeword and starts no other: w. So far: xw
111 is a codeword and starts no other: z. So far: xwz
110 is a codeword and starts no other: y. So far: xwzy

cards.title: In Python
cards.body: Time O(k) for k symbols. Entropy of this source is about 1.85 bits, so 1.9 is close but not perfect.

cards.title: The limit
cards.body: Shannon's first theorem: no code can average fewer bits per symbol than the source's entropy, and good codes get close. Shannon and Robert Fano built early codes; Fano's student David Huffman improved them. A Huffman code built with a heap takes O(k log k) time for k symbols.

visual.caption: Bits per symbol: the entropy floor, our code, and a plain 2-bit code

cards.title: The old answer
cards.body: Before Shannon, engineers fought noise mostly with power: send a stronger signal and shout over the static. Shannon turned this around: leave the channel as it is and change how you encode the message.

visual.caption: Shannon's cure sits at the two ends; the noisy channel is left alone

cards.title: Channel capacity
cards.body: Every channel has a capacity: the most bits per second it can carry reliably. It depends on the channel's bandwidth and its signal-to-noise ratio. This speed limit is called the Shannon limit.

visual.caption: Shannon's second theorem: capacity is the line between possible and not

cards.title: A repetition code
cards.body: Send each bit 3 times and take a majority vote of each block. One flipped copy per block gets fixed. Time O(n), but it triples the bits.

cards.title: Watch it work
cards.body: The code from the last card, run on the message 1, 0.

frames.caption: The message: two bits, 1 then 0
send() repeats each bit 3 times: six bits go out
Noise flips the first copy from 1 to 0
Block 1 holds 2 ones out of 3: the majority says 1
Block 2 holds 0 ones: the majority says 0
Decoded 1, 0: the flipped copy was outvoted and fixed
But two flips in one block win the vote: this decodes to 0, 0

cards.title: Finding the codes
cards.body: Smarter codes protect more for fewer extra bits than tripling everything.

events.what: Shannon shows good codes must exist, not how to build them
The search for those codes goes on
Codes finally come close to the Shannon limit

cards.title: The idea
cards.body: Big O describes how the work an algorithm does grows as its input grows. It counts steps, not seconds, so it compares algorithms, not computers. n is the input size. The same notation is used for memory.

visual.caption: log n stays almost flat while n² and 2ⁿ shoot off the top

cards.title: Doubling the input
cards.body: A quick test for any growth rate: double n and see what happens to the work.

visual.caption: Read across: what doubling n does to the step count

cards.title: Common run times
cards.body: A dict (hash table) lookup is O(1) on average. Slower still than this list: O(2ⁿ) and O(n!).

visual.caption: Fastest at the top, slowest at the bottom

cards.title: Counting with logs
cards.body: Here log n means log base 2: how many times n can be halved before it reaches 1. log₂ 1,024 is 10, so a thousand items give about 10 halvings and a million about 20.

frames.caption: 8 items to start with
Halve once: 4 left
Halve twice: 2 left
Halve three times: 1 left, so log₂ 8 = 3

cards.title: Steps at n = 16
cards.body: Plug a number in to feel the difference. 16 halves four times, so log n = 4.

visual.caption: Same n, very different amounts of work

cards.title: Why growth matters
cards.body: Growth rates pull apart quickly. Code that feels instant on a test list can crawl on real data if its growth rate is bad.

visual.caption: Bottom row: 20 steps against a trillion

cards.title: Single steps: O(1)
cards.body: A step whose cost doesn't depend on n is O(1): reading items[0], adding two numbers, returning a value. Indexing jumps straight to the slot, for ten items or ten million.

visual.caption: items[0] jumps straight to slot 0, however long the list is

cards.title: One loop: O(n)
cards.body: O(1) work on each of n items is n steps in total. It keeps only a variable or two: O(1) extra space.
cards.code:
for x in items:   # n passes
    print(x)      # O(1) each
# n × O(1) = O(n)

frames.caption: Pass 1 of 4: one O(1) step
Pass 2 of 4: one O(1) step
Pass 3 of 4: one O(1) step
Pass 4 of 4: one O(1) step; n items, n steps

cards.title: Nested loops multiply
cards.body: A loop inside a loop runs its body once per outer pass. Two loops over n give n × n = n², three give n³. Over lists of sizes n and m it is n × m, which is n² only when the sizes match.

frames.caption: Outer pass i = 0: 3 inner steps, 3 so far
Outer pass i = 1: 3 inner steps, 6 so far
Outer pass i = 2: 3 inner steps, 9 so far = 3 × 3

cards.title: Triangle loops
cards.body: If the inner loop runs up to the outer index, it runs 0, 1, 2, … n − 1 times. That adds up to n(n − 1)/2, about half of n², which is still O(n²).

visual.caption: 0 + 1 + 2 + 3 + 4 = 10 steps: about half of the 5 × 5 square

cards.title: Shapes to spot
cards.body: Doubling until done costs the same as halving. Trying every subset means each item is either in or out, which gives 2ⁿ combinations.

visual.caption: Spot the shape, then read off the cost

cards.title: Keep the big term
cards.body: Big O keeps only the term that grows fastest. For 4n³ + 2n + 9 the n³ term wins, so it is O(n³). At n = 1,000, n³ is a billion while 2n is only 2,000.

visual.caption: The n³ column dwarfs the rest, so only it is kept

cards.title: Drop the multiplier
cards.body: Constant factors don't change the shape of growth. 7n, n/3 and n steps are all O(n): doubling n doubles each. Several steps per pass, or skipping every other item, is still linear.

visual.caption: 7n, n and n/3 are all straight lines. Only n² bends upward

cards.title: Add or multiply
cards.body: Loops one after another add their costs. Loops inside each other multiply them.

visual.caption: A loop then nested loops: the n² part wins

cards.title: Rules of thumb
cards.body: Drop constant factors, drop smaller terms, and keep different inputs apart.

visual.caption: Constants and small terms go; different inputs stay apart

cards.title: When constants matter
cards.body: Constants are real work. With the same growth rate, less work per step wins. With different rates, the slower-growing one wins once n is big enough, however large its constant.

visual.caption: The scan's tiny constant only wins while n is small

cards.title: A worked example
cards.body: A takes 50·n steps, B takes n². B wins on tiny inputs (n = 10: 500 vs 100), they tie at n = 50 (2,500 each), then A pulls away for good (n = 500: 25,000 vs 250,000).

visual.caption: The lines cross at n = 50. After that B is always above A

cards.title: Quicksort vs merge sort
cards.body: Both sort in O(n log n) on average. Quicksort usually finishes first because its hidden constant is smaller. Merge sort never gets worse than O(n log n).

right.title: Merge sort
points: O(n log n) in every case

visual.caption: Same average growth rate; the smaller constant usually wins

cards.title: Best, worst, average
cards.body: The best case is the luckiest input, the worst case the unluckiest. Big O usually quotes the worst case: a promise that it is never slower than that.

frames.caption: Best case: looking for 7. It is first, 1 check: O(1)
Worst case: looking for 1. It is last, 6 checks: O(n)
Also worst: looking for 5. All 6 checked, no match: O(n)

cards.title: Quicksort's cases
cards.body: The numbers are sublist sizes, with the pivot taken out at each split. Every level touches up to n items, so cost = levels × n. A random pivot gives O(n log n) on average.

frames.caption: Even splits: 7 items need 3 levels, about log n. O(n log n)
Pivot always the smallest: 5 items need 5 levels. n levels, O(n²)

cards.title: Halving loops
cards.body: A loop that cuts n in half on each pass runs about log₂ n times. A counter that doubles from 1 up to n needs the same number of passes. Either way it keeps one counter: O(1) space.

visual.caption: n = 32 falls to 1 in 5 halvings: log₂ 32 = 5

frames.caption: Pass 1: i goes 1 → 2
Pass 2: i goes 2 → 4
Pass 3: i goes 4 → 8
Pass 4: i goes 8 → 16
Pass 5: i goes 16 → 32; 32 is not < 32, so stop after 5 passes

cards.title: Log inside a loop
cards.body: Put a halving or doubling loop inside a loop that runs n times and you get n × log n: O(n log n). Multiplying works because the inner loop does the same work on every outer pass.

visual.caption: n = 8: 8 outer passes × 3 inner passes = 24 steps

cards.title: When not to multiply
cards.body: If the inner work changes from pass to pass, add the passes up. An inner loop that runs 1, 2, 4, 8, … times up to n totals less than 2n: O(n), even though the outer loop runs log n times.

frames.caption: Inner loop runs 1 time: 1 in total
Inner loop runs 2 times: 3 in total
Inner loop runs 4 times: 7 in total
Inner loop runs 8 times: 15 in total
Inner loop runs 16 times: 31 in total, less than 2 × 32

cards.title: Memory grows too
cards.body: Space complexity measures the extra memory an algorithm needs on top of its input, with the same Big O rules.

right.title: O(n) extra
points: A new list, set or dict

visual.caption: Extra space counts memory on top of the input itself

cards.title: O(1) vs O(n)
Watch it grow
cards.body: doubled([3, 1, 4, 5]) fills a new list one slot per pass, while total keeps a single number t the whole way.

frames.caption: Pass 1: out holds 1 item
Pass 2: out holds 2 items
Pass 3: out holds 3 items
Pass 4: out holds 4 items; n items in, n slots used

cards.title: Running answers
cards.body: Many one-pass tasks need only a running answer: a sum, a count (start at 0, add 1 per match), the best so far. O(n) time, O(1) space. Storing extra wastes memory; sorting first costs O(n log n).

frames.caption: Start with best = the first item, 4
9 > 4, so best becomes 9
2 is not bigger than 9: best stays
7 is not bigger than 9: best stays
12 > 9, so best becomes 12
5 is not bigger than 12: best stays. Answer: 12

cards.title: Merge sort's buffer
cards.body: Merge sort combines two sorted halves into a temporary list. That buffer can hold all n items: O(n) extra space on top of O(n log n) time.

frames.caption: Take 1 from the right half [1, 4, 9]
Take 2 from the left half [2, 7, 8]
Take 4 from the right half [1, 4, 9]
Take 7 from the left half [2, 7, 8]
Take 8 from the left half [2, 7, 8]
Take 9: the buffer now holds all 6 items

cards.title: List operations
cards.body: `x in items` checks item by item. insert(0, x) and pop(0) make every other item shift over.

visual.caption: Cheap at the end of a list, costly at the front

cards.title: Why the front is slow
cards.body: A list stores its items side by side, so putting something at the front means sliding everything else along first.

frames.caption: insert(0, 'x'): slot 0 is taken, so make room
Move 9 one slot right
Move 2 one slot right
Move 8 one slot right
Move 5 one slot right
Now x fits. All 4 items had to move: O(n)

cards.title: Sets and dicts
cards.body: Sets and dicts are hash tables. The hash of a key points straight to its slot, so lookup, insert and `in` are O(1) on average. If many keys collide, an operation can degrade to O(n).

right.title: Set / dict
points: x in s, d[key]: O(1) on average
The hash points to the slot

visual.caption: Same question, very different cost

cards.title: Other handy tools
cards.body: bisect.bisect runs a binary search, so the list must already be sorted.

visual.caption: A deque is fast at both ends; a list only at the back

cards.title: Amortized append
cards.body: A list keeps spare room at its end. When it runs out, everything moves to a bigger block: O(n). The block grows in proportion to its size (drawn here as doubling), so n appends cost O(n) in all, O(1) each on average.

frames.caption: Append A: first block, size 1. Copies so far: 0
Append B: full, so move 1 to a block of 2. Copies so far: 1
Append C: full, so move 2 to a block of 4. Copies so far: 3
Append D: spare room, nothing moves. Copies so far: 3
Append E: full, so move 4 to a block of 8. Copies so far: 7

cards.title: Fixed growth fails
cards.body: Growing by a fixed number of slots means a move every few appends, each copying everything so far: 5 + 10 + 15 + … + n grows like n², so n appends cost O(n²) and each averages O(n).

visual.caption: 100 appends: 950 copies growing by 5 slots, 127 by doubling

cards.title: Hidden loops
cards.body: `x in some_list` and `some_list.count(x)` are loops in disguise. Called inside another loop over n items they turn O(n) work into O(n²).

visual.caption: Checks made by a loop that tests membership once per item (worst case)

cards.title: Trade memory for time
cards.body: Build a set once and each membership test becomes O(1) on average. O(n) time, O(n) space.

cards.title: Seen it before?
cards.body: A set of values seen so far answers 'have I met this already?' in one pass. Start empty; for each item, check the set first, then add the item. O(n) time, O(n) space.

frames.caption: 4 is new, add it: seen = {4}
7 is new, add it: seen = {4, 7}
1 is new, add it: seen = {4, 7, 1}
7 is already in seen: duplicate found, stop

cards.title: Tallying with a dict
cards.body: Read the current count with a default of 0 and store one more. Each update is O(1) on average: O(n) time, O(k) space for k distinct values.

frames.caption: Read 'kiwi': new key, 0 + 1 = 1
Read 'fig': new key, 0 + 1 = 1
Read 'kiwi': 1 + 1 = 2
Read 'plum': new key, 0 + 1 = 1
Read 'kiwi': 2 + 1 = 3

cards.title: Two pointers
cards.body: On a sorted list you can skip the extra memory. Start an index at each end, looking for a pair that sums to 13. Too small: move lo up. Too big: move hi down. Stop when they meet. O(n) time, O(1) space.

frames.caption: 1 + 9 = 10, too small: move lo up
3 + 9 = 12, too small: move lo up
4 + 9 = 13: found

cards.title: Time: count the calls
cards.body: For recursion, time is about (number of calls) × (work per call).

cards.title: Shrink or halve
cards.body: A function that calls itself once on n − 1 makes about n calls. One that calls itself once on n // 2 makes about log₂ n calls.

visual.caption: Counting calls down to the base case (n = 0 on the left, n = 1 on the right)

cards.title: Space: stack depth
cards.body: Every call waits on the call stack until the call it made returns. Extra space is the longest chain of waiting calls, not the total number of calls. Shrinking by one: depth n. Halving: depth log n.

frames.caption: total(a, 0) is called and pushed
total(a, 1) is called and pushed
total(a, 2) is called and pushed
Deepest point for 3 items: 4 calls on the stack, O(n) space
total(a, 3) returned 0 and was popped; the rest follow

cards.title: Hidden copies
cards.body: A slice like items[1:] builds a new list on every call. Over n calls the copies hold n − 1, n − 2, … items, about n²/2 steps: O(n²) time. Passing a start index keeps it O(n).

visual.caption: Items copied by each items[1:] when n = 6: 5 + 4 + 3 + 2 + 1 = 15

cards.title: Two calls on halves
cards.body: With O(1) work per call but two calls on half the input, the call tree has 1 + 2 + 4 + … + n nodes, about 2n: O(n) time, with a stack only log n deep.

visual.caption: f(8): 1 + 2 + 4 + 8 = 15 calls, about 2n, yet only 4 levels deep

cards.title: Reuse the half
cards.body: Compute the half once, reuse it, and there is one call per level: O(log n) time and stack. An odd n needs one extra multiply by x.

visual.caption: 2 to the power 10 takes 5 calls, not 11: one call per halving

cards.title: Writing T(n)
cards.body: A recurrence gives a recursive algorithm's cost in terms of smaller inputs. T(n) = 2T(n/2) + O(n) reads: two calls on halves, plus linear work to combine them.

visual.caption: T(n/2) + O(1): one call on a half plus constant work

cards.title: Levels times work
cards.body: Picture the call tree, count its levels and the work on each. Merge sort halves the list, so about log₂ n levels, each merging n items in all: O(n log n) in every case. One call on a half with O(1) work: O(log n).

frames.caption: Top level: one list of 8 to merge, 8 items of work
Next level: 4 + 4 = 8 items of work
Then 2 + 2 + 2 + 2 = 8 again
8 single items. 3 halvings, about 8 work each: n × log n

cards.title: Shrinking by one
cards.body: When each call shrinks n by 1 there are n levels. With O(1) work per level that is O(n). If each level scans what is left, the work is n + (n − 1) + … + 1: O(n²).

visual.caption: Each level scans what is left: 6 + 5 + 4 + 3 + 2 + 1 = 21, about n²/2

cards.title: Branching blows up
cards.body: Two calls that each shrink n by only one double the calls per level: 1, 2, 4, 8, … about 2ⁿ in total. Naive recursive Fibonacci works like this: exponential time.

visual.caption: fib(4) makes 9 calls and solves f(2) twice. fib(30) makes 2,692,537

cards.title: Caching fixes it
cards.body: When branches recompute the same inputs, store each result the first time. functools.cache does it for you: put @cache above the function.

cards.title: Each input once
cards.body: With the cache, grid(r, c) computes at most (r + 1)(c + 1) inputs. Uncached, grid(10, 10) makes 369,511 calls; cached, at most 121 inputs.

frames.caption: grid(1, 1) = 1 + 1 = 2, worked out once and stored
grid(2, 1) = 2 + 1 = 3: the 2 comes straight from the cache
grid(2, 2) = 3 + 3 = 6. Each cell was computed only once

cards.title: Every ordering
cards.body: Some problems seem to need every ordering: n stops have n! = n × (n − 1) × … × 1 orders. Brute force loops over each one, measures the route and keeps the shortest: O(n · n!), worse even than O(2ⁿ).

from itertools import permutations
stops = ["A", "B", "C", "D"]

cards.title: NP-complete problems
cards.body: The traveling salesperson problem and set cover are NP-complete. Nobody knows a fast exact algorithm for them, and most experts think none exists.

cards.title: Warning signs
cards.body: Suspect an NP-complete problem when the task is fast with a few items and hopeless with a few dozen, or when a known hard problem like set cover hides inside it.

cards.body: An approximation algorithm is fast and close to the best, but gives no promise that its answer is the best. They are judged by speed and closeness. Greedy rules make good ones, like always driving to the nearest unvisited stop.

cards.title: Why sort
cards.body: Sorting puts items in order so later jobs get easier: binary search, spotting duplicates, ranking. Most simple sorts work in passes. A pass is one sweep through the list.

frames.caption: Unsorted: finding a value means checking every bar
Sorted: order makes searching and ranking easy

cards.title: Stable sorts
cards.body: A sort is stable when items that count as equal keep the order they had before. Here cards are sorted by rank only; the letter is the suit. This matters when you sort by one field and then by another.

frames.caption: Before: 7h is left of 7c
Stable: the two 7s keep their order, 7h then 7c
Not stable: sorted by rank, but the 7s traded places

cards.title: More words
bullets: In place: rearranges the list itself, using only O(1) extra memory.
Adaptive: runs faster when the input is already nearly sorted.
Pivot: the item quicksort splits the list around.
Pass: one sweep through the list.

visual.caption: Five words that describe sorts

cards.title: Is it sorted?
cards.body: Compare each item with the one after it. One pair out of order means not sorted, so stop right there. With an index loop, stop at len(a) - 1 so a[i + 1] stays inside. Time O(n), extra space O(1).

def is_sorted(a):
    return all(x <= y for x, y
               in zip(a, a[1:]))

print(is_sorted([1, 4, 4, 9]))

cards.body: Find the smallest item in the unsorted part and swap it to the front of that part. Then do the same for the rest. After pass i, the first i + 1 items are in their final places.

cards.body: Walk along the list comparing neighbors and swap any pair where the left one is bigger. The largest item wins every comparison, so one pass carries it to the end. After pass i, the last i + 1 items are final.

After pass 3: the last 3 items are final

cards.body: a, b = b, a swaps two values in one line. j stops at n - 2 - i, so a[j + 1] stays inside the list and the sorted tail is skipped. A pass with no swaps means the list is sorted, so we stop early.

cards.title: The early exit
cards.body: A pass that makes no swaps proves the list is sorted. On a sorted list of n items that is one pass of n - 1 comparisons.

Comparison 3: 5 < 7, no swap
Comparison 4: 7 < 9, no swap

bullets: Without the early exit: (n-1) + (n-2) + ... + 1 comparisons, about n²/2.
Extra space O(1).
Stable, because it swaps only when the left item is strictly bigger (> not >=).

visual.caption: Only the early exit makes the best case O(n)

cards.title: The idea
cards.body: Keep a sorted part on the left. Take the next item (the key), shift every bigger item in the sorted part one slot right, and drop the key into the gap. It is how many people sort cards in their hand.

5 > 3: shift 5 one slot right
2 < 3: stop and drop 3 into the gap

cards.body: The while loop stops at index -1 or at an item that is not bigger than key. The gap is then at j + 1.

cards.title: Counting shifts
cards.body: Every shift fixes one pair that was out of order. A reversed list has the most such pairs, n(n - 1)/2: here 1 + 2 + 3 + 4 = 10 shifts. A sorted list needs 0 shifts.

frames.caption: Reversed: every pair is out of order
Insert 4: 1 shift, 1 so far
Insert 3: 2 shifts, 3 so far
Insert 2: 3 shifts, 6 so far
Insert 1: 4 shifts, 10 so far

bullets: Best case O(n) on sorted input; average and worst case O(n²).
O(1) extra space, stable, and adaptive.
The best simple choice for short or nearly sorted lists.

cards.title: Divide and conquer
cards.body: Divide and conquer (D&C) is a recursive way to solve problems. Find a base case so simple you can answer it straight away, and a way to shrink the problem until it reaches that base case. Binary search, merge sort and quicksort all work this way.

visual.caption: Work out two things: the base case and how to shrink toward it

cards.title: The plan
cards.body: Split the list in half, sort each half with merge sort, then merge the two sorted halves. A list of 0 or 1 items is already sorted: the base case. Halving 16 items goes 16, 8, 4, 2, 1: four levels, because 2⁴ = 16. In general: log₂ n levels.

visual.caption: Piece sizes for 8 items: each level halves them until every piece is 1

cards.title: Merging two halves
cards.body: Look only at the front item of each sorted half and take the smaller one. Repeat until one half is empty, then add the rest of the other. On a tie take the left item (<=), so equal items keep their order and the sort stays stable.

cards.title: A merge traced
cards.body: Merging [4, 7, 7] and [3, 7]. Taking the left item on a tie keeps equal items in order.

frames.caption: Compare only the two front items: 4 and 3
3 is smaller: take from the right
4 <= 7: take from the left
7 <= 7: take from the left (a tie goes left)
7 <= 7: take from the left (a tie goes left)
One half is empty: add the rest of the other

cards.title: The recursion
cards.body: Use // so mid is a whole number. Checking only len(a) == 0 would recurse forever on a 1-item list.

cards.title: What it costs
bullets: log n levels × O(n) per level = O(n log n) in the best, average and worst case.
O(n) extra space for the merged lists, so it is not in place.
Stable.

visual.caption: 8 items: every level moves all 8, and there are 3 levels

cards.title: The idea
cards.body: Pick one item as the pivot. Partition: move smaller items to its left and the rest to its right. The pivot is now in its final place. Sort the two sides the same way. Lists with fewer than 2 items are the base case.

frames.caption: Pick a pivot: here the first item, 5
Partitioned: 5 is final. The sides are not sorted yet
Sort each side the same way and the list is sorted

cards.title: Easy version
cards.code:
def quicksort(a):
    if len(a) < 2:
        return a
    p = a[0]
    rest = a[1:]
    s = [x for x in rest if x < p]
    b = [x for x in rest if x >= p]
    return (quicksort(s) + [p]
            + quicksort(b))
cards.body: Using >= keeps copies of the pivot; with > they would vanish. Any item can be the pivot: the middle value a[len(a) // 2] avoids bad splits on sorted input. New lists mean O(n) extra space.

cards.title: Three groups
cards.body: Another way to keep every copy of the pivot: a middle group [x for x in a if x == p], between the x < p and x > p groups. Only the outer groups are sorted again.

visual.caption: [4, 9, 4, 1, 7] with the middle item 4 as pivot p

cards.title: In-place partition
cards.body: The last item is the pivot. i marks where the next small item goes. The final swap drops the pivot between the groups. O(n) time, O(1) space.

cards.title: A partition traced

2 < 4: swap a[i] and a[j], then i moves right
9 is not < 4: leave it
1 < 4: swap a[i] and a[j], then i moves right
Swap the pivot into slot i: returns 2

cards.title: The recursion
cards.body: Both calls leave out index p, because the pivot is already in place. Passing p again could repeat the same range forever.

visual.caption: Index ranges sorted for [7, 2, 9, 1, 4]: the pivot's index is never passed down

cards.title: Work per level
cards.body: Picture the recursion as levels. On every level, the partitions together touch about all n items, so each level costs O(n). Total time is n times the number of levels.

visual.caption: Sizes of the pieces with even splits of 15 items: only 4 levels

cards.title: Good and bad splits
bullets: Even splits: about log n levels, so O(n log n) time and O(log n) stack.
Pivot is always the smallest or largest: sides of 0 and n - 1, so n levels: O(n²) time, O(n) stack.
A first-item pivot on a list that is already sorted does exactly that.

visual.caption: Worst pivots on 5 items: sides of 0 and n - 1, so 5 levels

cards.title: Choosing a pivot
cards.body: Use the middle item or a random one. No fixed input can force bad splits on a random pivot every time, so the expected time is O(n log n). random.randint(lo, hi) includes both ends; swap the chosen item to the end, then partition.

frames.caption: Sorted input, first item as pivot: sides of 0 and 6
Middle item as pivot: sides of 3 and 3
Random pivot: the O(n²) worst case can still happen, but it is very unlikely

cards.title: Many duplicates
cards.body: A three-way partition makes three groups: less than, equal to, and greater than the pivot. The equal group is done and never sorted again, so a list of all-equal items takes O(n). It does not fix a bad pivot on sorted input.

frames.caption: Pivot value 3 appears four times
Less | equal | greater: the four 3s are finished

cards.title: Versus merge sort
cards.body: Both are O(n log n) on average. Quicksort is usually faster in practice: its constant factor is smaller, and with random pivots it almost always hits the average case.

left.title: Quicksort
points: O(n log n) average, O(n²) worst

right.title: Merge sort
points: O(n log n) in every case

cards.title: What a heap is
cards.body: A max-heap is a tree where every parent is at least as big as its children, so the largest item is the root. It fits in a plain list: root at index 0, children of i at 2i + 1 and 2i + 2, parent at (i - 1) // 2.

frames.caption: Stored level by level as [9, 7, 8, 3, 5, 2]; the max is the root
7 is at index 1; its children are at 2·1+1 = 3 and 2·1+2 = 4

cards.title: Sift down
cards.body: Swap a[i] with its bigger child until it is bigger than both. O(log n), since a heap has about log n levels.

cards.title: Heapsort steps
cards.body: Build the heap from the last parent back to the root: O(n). Then swap the max to the end, shrink the heap by one, and repair the root.

cards.title: Steps traced
cards.body: heap_sort on [3, 9, 2, 7, 8, 5]. The heap shrinks from the right as the green sorted part grows.

frames.caption: Start: an ordinary list, not a heap yet
Heap built: the max, 9, is at index 0
Swap 9 to the end, repair: new root is 8
Swap 8 to the end, repair: new root is 7
Swap 7 to the end, repair: new root is 5
Swap 5 to the end, repair: new root is 3
Swap 3 into place: the list is sorted

cards.title: With heapq
cards.body: Python's heapq is a min-heap. heapify(a) builds it in O(n); heappop(a) removes the smallest item in O(log n). Popping n times gives sorted order, but into a new list: O(n) extra space. Prints [1, 4, 5].

The usual pick when you need a guarantee and no extra memory.

cards.title: Count, don't compare
cards.body: For whole numbers from 0 to k, counting sort tallies how often each value appears in a list of k + 1 counters, then writes each value out that many times. Counts [1, 1, 0, 2] read back as [0, 1, 3, 3].

frames.caption: Read 3: add 1 to the counter for 3
Read 1: add 1 to the counter for 1
Read 3: add 1 to the counter for 3
Read 0: add 1 to the counter for 0

cards.title: In Python
cards.body: k + 1 slots, so the value k has a slot of its own.

bullets: O(n + k) time and O(n + k) space in every case; k is the size of the value range.
No item is ever compared with another.

right.title: Poor fit

cards.title: Radix sort
cards.body: Sort by the ones digit, then the tens, then higher digits. Each pass keeps ties in the order they already had.

frames.caption: Start
By ones digit (0, 1, 3, 3): 23 stays ahead of 13
By tens digit (1, 2, 3, 4): sorted

cards.title: Why passes must be stable
cards.body: When two numbers share the current digit, their order must still show the lower digits sorted earlier. So each pass uses a stable sort, usually counting sort. With d digits and k digit values: O(d × (n + k)) time, O(n + k) space.

frames.caption: After the ones pass: 21 is ahead of 23
Stable tens pass: 21 and 23 tie on 2 and keep that order

cards.body: Python sorts with Timsort, a blend of merge sort and insertion sort. It finds runs that are already in order, sorts short pieces with insertion sort, and merges the runs. A sorted list is one long run: n - 1 comparisons and nothing to merge.

cards.title: Core ideas
bullets: Bubble: compare neighbors and swap any out-of-order pair.
Selection: each pass, find the minimum of the rest and put it next.
Insertion: grow a sorted left part one item at a time.
Merge: halve, sort both halves, merge them. Quick: split around a pivot item.
Heap: keep removing the max from a heap. Counting: count each value.

cards.title: Costs side by side
cards.body: Insertion sort's best case is O(n). Quicksort also uses an O(log n) stack. Counting sort is O(n + k) and compares nothing.

visual.caption: Merge and heap never get worse than O(n log n)

cards.title: The n log n floor
cards.body: A sort that only compares two items at a time needs about n log n comparisons in the worst case. There are n! possible orders, and each yes/no comparison at best halves those still possible. Counting and radix sort dodge this by not comparing.

visual.caption: Worst-case comparisons needed: log₂(n!) rounded up, which grows like n log₂ n

cards.title: Which to pick
bullets: Small, almost-sorted input: insertion sort, close to O(n).
Need stable and a guaranteed O(n log n): merge sort.
Need that guarantee with O(1) extra memory: heapsort.
Many whole numbers in a tiny range: counting sort.
Speed on average, in place, stability not needed: quicksort.

cards.title: The idea
cards.body: Check the items one by one from the start and stop at the first match. It works on any list, sorted or not. It is also called simple search. A missing item is only known to be missing after every item has been checked.

frames.caption: 4 is not 9: move on
7 is not 9: move on
1 is not 9: move on

cards.body: Return -1 only after the loop, once nothing matched. == compares; a single = assigns. A yes/no version returns True inside the loop and False after it.

cards.title: Python does it too
cards.body: in and .index() check items one by one from index 0; .index() gives the first match. find() gives -1 when the text is missing. min() and max() scan every item.

cards.title: Finding the smallest
cards.body: Start with best = a[0], then look at every item and replace best whenever you see a smaller one. Flip the test to > for the largest. This search can never stop early: O(n) in every case.

cards.title: The idea
cards.body: On a sorted list, look at the middle item. If it is the target, done. If it is bigger than the target, only the left half can hold the target; if smaller, keep the right half. Each check throws away half. Unsorted data breaks this.

mid + 1 and mid - 1: a[mid] is already ruled out, so leave it out.

cards.body: Same O(log n) time, but each call waits on the stack: O(log n) space instead of O(1).

cards.body: The same miss, recursively. Each call waits for the one above it, so the stack holds O(log n) calls where the loop needs O(1) space.

cards.title: Two classic bugs
bullets: lo = mid instead of mid + 1: with lo = 0, hi = 1, mid stays 0 and the loop never ends.
while lo < hi with hi = len(a) - 1: the last item left is never checked, so search([1, 2], 2) returns -1.

Nothing changed, so the loop never ends. lo = mid + 1 fixes it

cards.title: Insert positions
cards.body: Often you want where a value belongs. bisect_left(a, x) gives the first index whose item is >= x: before any copies of x. bisect_right(a, x) gives the first index whose item is > x: after the copies. Both are binary searches.

cards.body: To find a pair with a given sum in a sorted list, put one pointer at each end. Sum too small: move the left pointer right to a bigger item. Sum too big: move the right pointer left. Stop when they meet, so an item is never paired with itself.

cards.title: Fixed-size window
cards.body: For sums of k neighbors in a row, slide instead of re-adding: add the item that enters and subtract the one that leaves. When a[i] enters, a[i - k] falls out. Each slide is O(1).

Slide: add 3, subtract 7: sum 12. Best is 16

cards.title: In Python
cards.code:
def best_window(a, k):
    w = sum(a[:k])
    best = w
    for i in range(k, len(a)):
        w += a[i] - a[i - k]
        best = max(best, w)
    return best

a = [2, 7, 1, 8, 3]
print(best_window(a, 3))
cards.body: Windows of 3: 10, 16, 12. Prints 16.

cards.title: Slide or re-add
cards.body: Both find the best sum of k neighbors; the window just reuses the last total.

visual.caption: Reusing the running total removes the factor of k

cards.title: Grow and shrink
bullets: For a window of any size over positive numbers: hi moves right, adding a[hi].
While the window breaks the rule (say, sum > k): subtract a[lo] first, then lo += 1.
Now lo..hi is valid and holds hi - lo + 1 items.
Each index enters once and leaves at most once: O(n) time despite the inner loop, O(1) space.

cards.title: What rotation does
cards.body: A rotated list is a sorted list cut in two with the pieces swapped. It has exactly one drop. Pick any middle: the drop sits on at most one side, so at least one half is in sorted order.

frames.caption: A sorted list
Cut after 6 and swap the pieces: one drop, from 15 to 1
Middle index 2: the left half 10, 12, 15 is sorted; the drop is on the right

cards.title: The rule
bullets: If a[lo] <= a[mid], the left half is sorted. The = matters: when lo == mid, the left half is one item, which is sorted.
Otherwise the right half is sorted.
Is the target inside the sorted half's range? Search there; if not, search the other half.
Half is dropped each step: O(log n) time, O(1) space.

a[lo] 3 <= a[mid] 6: left is sorted. 3 is in 3..6: go left
mid = 4: found 3

cards.title: Which half
cards.body: The right half [1, 2, 3] is sorted, 6 is not in it, so go left.

cards.title: Smallest item
cards.body: The smallest item sits just after the drop. Compare a[mid] with a[hi]: if a[mid] > a[hi], lo = mid + 1; else hi = mid. Loop while lo < hi. Comparing with a[lo] instead fails on a list that isn't rotated.

a[mid] 11 > a[hi] 2: the drop is right of mid, lo = 2

cards.title: The idea
cards.body: Sometimes you search a range of possible answers, not a list: a speed, a size, a capacity. If a yes/no check ok(x) is False for every x that is too small and True from some point on, binary search can find that switch point.

cards.title: Round the middle up
cards.body: When you want the largest x that passes, the update is lo = mid. Then mid must round up, (lo + hi + 1) // 2. Otherwise, once hi = lo + 1, mid equals lo, nothing changes and the loop never ends.

bullets: About log₂(range) checks. For answers 1 to M: about log₂ M.
If one check scans n items: O(n log M) time.
Trying every value instead: O(n · M). Extra space O(1).

cards.title: Search in rings
cards.body: Breadth-first search (BFS) searches a graph outward from a start node, one ring at a time. It answers: is there a path to the goal, and which path has the fewest steps? Depth-first search instead follows one path as far as it goes before backing up.

frames.caption: Start at S
Ring 1: every node 1 step away
Ring 2: every node 2 steps away
Ring 3: G. The fewest steps from S to G is 3

cards.title: Why a queue
cards.body: BFS keeps the nodes still to check in a queue: first in, first out. Near nodes come out before far ones, so the first time the goal comes out its distance is the smallest. A stack (last in, first out) would dive deep and could find a longer path first.

frames.caption: Start: the queue holds only S
Take S from the front; add A and B at the back
Take A from the front; add C at the back
Take B from the front; add D at the back
Take C from the front; add G at the back
Take D from the front; all its neighbors were seen
G comes out: goal reached, 3 steps from S

cards.title: Mark what you've seen
cards.body: In a graph with a cycle, a node can be added to the queue again and again. That wastes work and can loop forever. Keep a set of seen nodes and add each node to the queue only once.

visual.caption: A cycle: A leads to B, B to C, and C back to A. Without a seen set, A is queued again

cards.title: In Python
cards.body: Each queue entry carries its distance; a neighbor is one step farther.

cards.title: Cost and limits
bullets: Time O(V + E): every node and edge is handled once. Space O(V).
Fewest steps means fewest edges, not lowest total cost.
When edges have different costs, such as road lengths, use Dijkstra's algorithm instead.

visual.caption: BFS takes S-G: 1 edge but cost 9. S-A-G has 2 edges and costs only 4

cards.title: The idea
cards.body: k-nearest neighbors (kNN) answers a question about a new item by finding the k stored items most like it. Classification: they vote and the most common label wins, like spam or not spam. Regression: average their numbers to predict a number, like a price.

visual.caption: k = 3: the three closest items vote 2 spam to 1 ok, so ? is labeled spam

cards.title: Items as features
cards.body: To compare items, turn each one into a list of numbers called features, like a used car's (age in years, thousands of km). Pick features that relate to what you predict. Put them on similar scales (say 0 to 1), or the feature with the biggest numbers swamps the rest.

visual.caption: Raw km differences dwarf age differences; scaled, both run from 0 to 1

cards.title: Measuring distance
cards.body: Straight-line distance: square each difference, add them, take the square root. Prints 5.0. It works for any number of features. math.dist does the same.

cards.title: Picking k
bullets: k = 1 trusts a single neighbor, which may be noise.
A bigger k gives smoother, steadier answers.
k = all items always predicts the overall most common label.
With two labels, an odd k means the vote can't tie.

frames.caption: k = 1: one neighbor decides. It says ok, but it may be noise
k = 3: 2 spam to 1 ok. A steadier answer: spam
k = all 7: 4 ok to 3 spam. Always the overall most common label

Each prediction computes n distances: O(n · d).

cards.title: The toolbox
bullets: Linear search: look at each item in turn; no order needed. O(n).
Binary search: cut a sorted range in half every step. O(log n).
Two pointers: one index at each end, moving inward. O(n).
Sliding window: keep a running total as a range of neighbors moves along. O(n).
Hash lookup: hash the key to go directly to its bucket. O(1) average.

cards.title: Sort first?
cards.body: Sorting costs O(n log n), more than one O(n) scan. For a single search of unsorted data, just scan. For many searches, sort once and then each binary search is O(log n). Trying every pair of items is O(n²), which these tools usually avoid.

visual.caption: 1,000 items: sorting first pays off after about 10 searches

cards.title: Spot the pattern
bullets: Minimum size that still succeeds, when anything larger succeeds too: binary search over the answer range.
Sorted data that was cut and swapped: binary search that tests which half is in order.
Longest stretch of neighbors under a limit: a window that grows and shrinks.
Fewest moves through a maze or network: BFS, O(V + E).
Membership checks, like a name seen already: a hash set.

cards.title: Nodes and edges
cards.body: A graph is a set of things, called nodes or vertices, joined by links called edges. Two nodes joined by an edge are neighbors. The degree of a node is how many edges touch it. Road maps and friend networks are graphs.

visual.caption: Three edges touch c, so its degree is 3. Its neighbors are a, b and d

cards.title: Kinds of graphs
cards.body: Tap through the kinds. One graph can be several at once, such as directed and weighted.

frames.caption: Directed: every edge is a one-way arrow (a follows b)
Undirected: every edge works both ways (a and b are cousins)
Weighted: every edge carries a cost, like minutes or dollars
Connected: every node can reach every other node
Not connected: c and d cannot reach a, b or e
Sparse: far fewer edges than possible pairs of nodes (4 of 10 here)
Dense: most of the possible pairs are joined (9 of 10 here)

cards.title: Paths and cycles
cards.body: A path is a chain of edges leading from one node to another. A cycle is a path that ends at the node where it started. Searches have to watch out for cycles, or they can walk around one forever.

frames.caption: A path: the chain of edges a, b, d, e leads from a to e
A cycle: a, b, d, c and back to a. It ends where it started

cards.title: Trees are graphs
cards.body: A tree is a connected graph with no cycles, so there is exactly one path between any two nodes. With n nodes it always has n − 1 edges: every node except the root hangs from one edge to its parent.

frames.caption: A tree: 5 nodes, 4 edges, one path between any two nodes
Joining c and d, already linked through a, adds a second path: a cycle
Joining a brand-new node e keeps it a tree: 6 nodes, 5 edges

cards.title: Degree in Python
cards.body: When each node maps to a list of its neighbors, len() of that list is the node's degree, in O(1) time.

visual.caption: g['a'] lists b, c and d, so len() gives a degree of 3

cards.title: Adjacency list
cards.body: Map each node to a list of its neighbors. Memory is O(V + E): one entry per node plus one per edge. Listing neighbors is quick, but checking for one particular edge scans that node's list, O(degree).

visual.caption: c's list is a, b, d. Each edge shows up in two lists: 8 entries, 4 edges

cards.body: A V × V grid where m[u][v] is 1 when the edge u → v exists (or holds its weight). Edge check: read one cell, O(1). Neighbors: scan a whole row, O(V). Memory: O(V²), even when almost no edges exist.

cards.title: The idea
cards.body: BFS spreads out from the start in rings: every node one edge away, then two, and so on. The first time it reaches a node, it used the fewest possible edges. Use it for "is there a path?" and for shortest paths in an unweighted graph.

Ring 1: a and b are one edge from s
Ring 2: c, d and e are two edges from s
Ring 3: f, three edges away. Visit order: s a b c d e f

cards.title: Why a queue
cards.body: Nodes are handled in the order they were found, so BFS keeps a first-in, first-out queue: take from the front, add to the back. Use collections.deque: popleft() is O(1), list.pop(0) is O(n). Taking from the back instead (a stack) gives DFS.

Take s from the front; add its new neighbors a, b at the back
Take a from the front; add its new neighbors c, d at the back
Take b from the front; add its new neighbor e at the back
Take c from the front; it has no new neighbors
Take d from the front; add its new neighbor f at the back
Take e from the front; it has no new neighbors

cards.title: Remember what you saw
cards.body: Keep a set of the nodes already found and mark each node as you add it to the queue. Without it, a node reachable two ways is handled twice, and a cycle keeps the search going around forever.

cards.body: DFS follows one path as deep as it can, then backs up to the latest fork and tries the next branch. It runs on a stack (last in, first out): a list with append() and pop(), or the call stack through recursion. It reaches every node it can, but not by the shortest route.

cards.body: A connected component is a group of nodes that can all reach each other; a node with no edges is one by itself. Loop over every node and start a new DFS (or BFS) from each one no earlier search reached. Each new start is one more component.

cards.title: Spotting cycles
cards.body: Undirected: every edge shows up from both ends, so only a seen neighbor other than the node you came from means a cycle. Directed: track unvisited, in progress (on the current path) and finished.

Directed: a, b, c are in progress. Edge c → a hits an in-progress node: a cycle
Directed: b and c are finished when a checks a → c. A finished node: no cycle

cards.body: Let an arrow a → b mean "a must happen before b". A topological sort lists every node before all the nodes it points to. Several orders are often valid. It only works on a directed graph with no cycles (a DAG): in a cycle each task waits on another forever.

cards.title: Cheapest, not fewest
cards.body: With costs on the edges, the cheapest route can use more edges than the BFS route. Dijkstra's finds the cheapest total cost from a start to every node. Repeat: pick the unfinished node with the smallest known cost, call it finished, and try to improve its neighbors through it.

Next is b (5). Through b, t drops from 9 to 5 + 1 = 6
t finishes at 6 by s, a, b, t: three edges beat the single edge that costs 9

cards.title: Dijkstra setup
cards.body: Distances start at infinity. The heap holds (distance, node) pairs, so it orders them by distance. The table traces what the loop on the next card does with this graph.

frames.caption: Start: only s has a cost, and the heap holds (0, s)
Pop (5, a): no neighbors to improve
Pop (7, a): 7 > dist[a] = 5, a stale entry, so it is skipped

cards.title: The main loop
cards.body: Continues the setup. Relaxing: when going through node is cheaper, save the new cost and push it. Old pairs for that node stay in the heap and are skipped when popped.

cards.title: Rebuilding the route
cards.body: Each time you improve a node n, also save parent[n] = node. The start's parent is None. Begin at the goal and keep stepping to the parent, collecting nodes until you run out. The list is goal-first, so reverse it.

frames.caption: path = [t]. parent[t] is b, so step to b
path = [t, b]. parent[b] is a, so step to a
path = [t, b, a]. parent[a] is s, so step to s
path = [t, b, a, s]. parent[s] is None: stop. Reversed: s, a, b, t

cards.title: Negative edges break it
cards.body: A finished node is never revisited. That is safe when all weights are 0 or more: any other route already costs at least as much before it arrives. A negative edge can make a costlier detour end up cheaper, and the finished node misses it. Use Bellman-Ford then.

frames.caption: Finish s: a costs 3 and b costs 4
a (3) is the smallest, so a is finished at 3
Then b: s, b, a costs 4 − 2 = 2, but a is already finished at 3. Wrong

cards.title: What it costs
bullets: Works on directed or undirected graphs, cycles included, when no weight is negative.

visual.caption: Scanning every node for the cheapest skips the heap but costs O(V²)

cards.title: The idea
cards.body: Bellman-Ford finds cheapest paths from a start even when some edges are negative. It has no heap and never calls a node finished. It simply relaxes every edge, round after round, keeping any shorter distance it finds.

visual.caption: s → b → a costs 1 − 2 = −1, cheaper than the direct edge that costs 4

cards.title: Why V − 1 rounds
cards.body: A cheapest path never needs to visit a node twice, so it has at most V − 1 edges. Each full round over all edges locks in at least one more edge of every cheapest path. After V − 1 rounds every distance is correct.

frames.caption: Path s → a → b → c (3, −1, 2). Edges are checked in the worst order: b→c, a→b, s→a
Round 1: only s → a can improve anything, so a = 3
Round 2: a → b now works, so b = 3 − 1 = 2
Round 3: b → c gives c = 2 + 2 = 4. V − 1 = 3 rounds, all correct

cards.title: In Python
Negative cycles
cards.body: Run one extra round. If any distance still drops, some loop has a negative total: going around it again keeps lowering the cost, so no cheapest path exists. That is how Bellman-Ford reports a reachable negative cycle.

frames.caption: The loop a → b → c → a adds up to 1 − 3 + 1 = −1
Costs after V − 1 = 3 rounds
The extra round still lowers b, c, a: a negative cycle is reported

cards.title: What it costs
cards.body: Time O(V × E): V − 1 rounds over E edges. Space O(V) for the distances. It is slower than Dijkstra's, so use it when negative edges exist.

left.title: Dijkstra's
points: O((V + E) log V) with a heap

visual.caption: Pay the slower O(V × E) only when an edge can be negative

cards.title: The idea
cards.body: Union-find (disjoint sets) tracks which items belong together while groups keep merging. Each item points to a parent; following parents up leads to the group's root, which names the group. Two items share a group exactly when they have the same root.

visual.caption: Arrows point to parents. c's root is r and d's root is q: different groups

cards.title: In Python
Merging step by step
cards.body: The code above at work. union() finds both roots and points one at the other.

frames.caption: Four items, each its own root: four groups
union(a, b): root a now points to root b. Three groups
union(c, d): c points to d. Two groups
union(a, c): their roots are b and d, so b is hung under d. One group
union(a, d) returns False: both already have root d

cards.title: Path compression
cards.body: While find walks up to the root, it points each node it passes straight at the root. That is the line parent[x] = find(parent[x]). Later finds from those nodes take a single step.

frames.caption: Before: find(w) climbs three steps, w to x to y to the root z
After: w and x point straight at z. The next find(w) takes one step

cards.title: Union by rank
cards.body: Keep a rank (a bound on height) for each root. Hang the root with the lower rank under the one with the higher rank, so the tree gets no taller. Only when the ranks are equal does the new root's rank go up by 1. That alone keeps every tree O(log n) tall.

frames.caption: Three roots: p and x have rank 1, r has rank 0
Join r and p: rank 0 hangs under rank 1. The tree is no taller, p stays rank 1
Join p and x: equal ranks, so x hangs under p and p's rank goes up to 2

cards.title: What it costs
cards.body: With both tricks, each find or union takes nearly constant amortized time; the bound grows so slowly it stays below 5 for any real input. Without them a group can become a long chain. Space is O(n) for parent and rank.

visual.caption: Nearly O(1) is amortized: averaged over a long run of calls

cards.title: The idea
cards.body: A spanning tree of a connected, undirected, weighted graph links all V nodes with V − 1 edges and no cycles. A minimum spanning tree (MST) is one whose edge weights add up to the least possible. Think of laying cable to reach every building as cheaply as possible.

visual.caption: The 4 highlighted edges reach all 5 nodes for 1 + 2 + 3 + 5 = 11, the least possible

cards.title: Kruskal's algorithm
cards.body: Sort the edges from cheapest to dearest. Keep an edge unless its two ends are already in one group (it would close a cycle); union-find makes that check fast. Stop once V − 1 edges are kept.

frames.caption: Cheapest edge: b-c (1). Its ends are in different groups: keep
Next: a-c (2). Its ends are in different groups: keep
Next: d-e (3). Its ends are in different groups: keep
a-b (4): a and b are already in one group. It would close a cycle: skip
c-d (5): keep. That is V − 1 = 4 edges, so stop. Total 11

cards.title: Kruskal in Python

# union() from the union-find note
E = [('a', 'b', 4), ('b', 'c', 1),
     ('a', 'c', 2), ('c', 'd', 5)]
E.sort(key=lambda e: e[2])
tree = []
for u, v, w in E:
    if union(u, v):
        tree.append((u, v, w))
print(tree)  # b-c, a-c, c-d: 8

cards.title: Prim's algorithm
cards.body: Prim's grows a single tree from a start node. Each step adds the cheapest edge that joins a node in the tree to a node outside it; a min-heap of candidate edges makes that pick fast. Kruskal's and Prim's always reach the same minimum total weight.

Cheapest edge leaving the tree: a-c (2). Add c
Cheapest edge leaving the tree: c-b (1). Add b
Cheapest edge leaving the tree: c-d (5). Add d
Last: d-e (3). All 5 nodes joined, total 11, same as Kruskal's

cards.title: What it costs
cards.body: Every spanning tree on V nodes has exactly V − 1 edges, whichever algorithm builds it.

visual.caption: Kruskal's time is mostly the sort of the edges

cards.title: When no fast way exists
cards.body: Some graph problems have no known fast exact method. The traveling salesperson problem asks for the shortest tour that visits every city once. Trying every possible order of n cities means about n! tours. Problems like this are called NP-complete.

visual.caption: 10 cities already give 3,628,800 orders to try

cards.title: Good enough, fast
cards.body: A greedy approximation: always go to the closest city not visited yet. O(n²) time, O(n) space. Usually short, not always the shortest.

cards.title: How memory works
cards.body: Memory is a long row of numbered slots; each slot's number is its address. An array keeps its items in one unbroken block, side by side (contiguous). Item i lives at the start address plus i times the item size, so reading any index is one jump, O(1): random access.

visual.caption: Start 1000, 8 bytes each: item 3 is at 1000 + 3 × 8 = 1024

cards.title: When an array fills
cards.body: To grow, an array may have to move: find a bigger free block and copy every item there, O(n). Dynamic arrays such as Python's list reserve spare slots and grow by a factor, so append averages O(1) (amortized), at the cost of some unused memory.

frames.caption: The slot right after the array already holds other data
Move: copy all 3 items into a bigger free block, O(n)
Spare slots are reserved, so the next appends just fill one: O(1)

cards.title: Linked lists
cards.body: Nodes can sit anywhere in memory. Each holds a value and a link to the next node; the list keeps the head. Reaching item i means following i links from the head, O(n): sequential access.

visual.caption: Reaching 3 means following two links from the head

cards.title: Insert and delete
cards.body: Next to a node you already hold, adding or removing changes one or two links, O(1). Push at the front: link the new node to the old head first, then make it the head (the other order loses the list). To drop the node after prev, point prev's link past it.

frames.caption: A list with its head at 1
Push 0 at the front: 0 links to the old head, then becomes the head
Now drop 2, the node right after prev
prev.next = prev.next.next: 1 now links straight to 3

cards.title: Arrays must shift
cards.body: An array has no links to change. To insert or delete anywhere but the end, every later item moves one slot, O(n).

frames.caption: Insert 0 at the front of this array
All 4 items shift one slot to the right: O(n)
Only now is slot 0 free for the new item

cards.body: The linked list's O(1) holds once you already hold the node before the spot.

cards.title: Last in, first out
cards.body: A stack lets you touch only its top. Push puts an item on top and pop takes the top item off, so the newest item always leaves first (LIFO), like a pile of plates. Both are O(1). Undo history works this way: the latest action is undone first.

frames.caption: J was pushed first, then K on top of it
Push L: it goes on top
Pop takes L, the newest. J, the oldest, will leave last

s.append('b')
print(s.pop())  # b
print(s[-1])    # a, the new top

cards.title: Too deep
cards.body: Recursion pushes one frame per call, so depth n costs O(n) memory. A function that never reaches a base case keeps pushing until Python stops it with RecursionError (the default limit is 1,000 frames). The fix is a base case, or a loop instead.

cards.title: First in, first out

cards.title: Hash functions
cards.body: A hash function turns a key into a number. It must be consistent: the same key always gives the same number, or you could never find what you stored. A good one also spreads different keys evenly over the slots, so few of them share one.

visual.caption: Toy hash: add up the letter codes. The same key gives the same number every time

cards.title: Array plus hash
cards.body: % folds any hash into a valid bucket index.

cards.title: Handling collisions
cards.body: Two different keys can land in the same bucket: a collision. Chaining keeps a small list in each bucket; open addressing probes for another free slot. A few are normal. If every key lands in one bucket, each lookup scans one long list, no better than a linked list.

visual.caption: With the toy hash, fig and plum both land in bucket 6: a collision

cards.title: Load factor
cards.body: Load factor = items ÷ buckets. As it rises, so do collisions. A common rule: once it passes about 0.7, make an array twice as big and re-insert every item, O(n). Since the size doubles, resizes are rare, so inserts still average O(1) (amortized).

frames.caption: 2 items ÷ 4 buckets: load factor 0.5
A third item: 3 ÷ 4 = 0.75, past 0.7, so it is time to grow
Twice the buckets, every item re-inserted, O(n). Now 3 ÷ 8 = 0.375

cards.title: What it costs
cards.body: The worst case comes from keys piling into one bucket. A good hash function and a low load factor keep you at the average. Space is O(n).

visual.caption: Worst case: every key in one bucket, so one long chain to scan

cards.title: Catching repeats
cards.body: Keep everything you've seen in a set and test each new item against it before adding it: n items cost O(n) time and O(n) space. Testing against a list rescans it every time, O(n²) in total. set(items) also drops duplicates in one go, without keeping order.

cards.title: Caching slow answers
cards.body: A cache remembers slow answers, keyed by the request. Look there first. Hit: return the saved answer. Miss: do the slow work, save the result under its key, then return it. The cache must live outside the function, or it is lost after each call.

cards.title: Tree words
cards.body: A tree starts at one root node, and each node links down to its children. In a binary tree every node has at most two children, left and right. A node with no children is a leaf. The height is the number of levels on the longest path from the root down.

visual.caption: 9 is the root. 2, 7 and 12 have no children: leaves. Three levels: height 3

cards.title: The BST rule
cards.body: All keys in a node's left subtree are smaller than its key; all keys in its right subtree are larger. To search, compare and go left or right, ignoring the other side, much like binary search. To insert, follow the same path and attach the new node where it falls off (at None).

7 > 5, so go right
Found 7 after 3 comparisons, one per level
Insert 11: 11 > 9 go right, 11 < 14 go left, 11 < 12 go left: nothing there
11 is attached where the search fell off, as 12's left child

cards.title: Search in Python
cards.body: A recursive insert returns each subtree's root, so the parent relinks it: node.left = insert(node.left, key).

cards.title: Balance matters
cards.body: Search and insert cost O(h) for height h. A balanced tree has h about log₂ n: O(log n). Sorted-order inserts into a plain BST all go right: a chain of height n, O(n), like a linked list. Self-balancing trees (AVL, red-black) rearrange nodes to keep h at O(log n).

The same keys inserted as 1, 2, 3, 4, 5: every one goes right. Height 5

cards.title: BST vs sorted array

Inorder: left subtree, the node, right subtree.

cards.title: The idea
cards.body: A min-heap is a binary tree where every parent is less than or equal to its children, so the smallest item is always at the root. It is not fully sorted; it only promises the top. Heaps power priority queues: always handle the most urgent item next.

cards.title: Stored in a list
cards.body: A heap fills its tree row by row, so it fits in a plain list with no links. With the root at index 0, the children of index i are at 2i + 1 and 2i + 2, and its parent is at (i − 1) // 2.

cards.title: Bloom filter
cards.body: A bit array plus k hash functions; it stores no items. Add: set the k bits the item's hashes point to. Check: read those k bits. Any 0 means it was never added; all 1s means it was probably added, since other items may have set the same bits.

Add dog: its hashes point to bits 4 and 3, so set both

Check cow: bits 9 and 2 are both 1. "Probably", yet never added

cards.title: Counting with HyperLogLog
cards.body: HyperLogLog estimates how many distinct items a huge stream holds, like unique visitors, without storing them. It hashes each item and keeps only small summaries of the hash patterns. Memory stays small and fixed; the count is close, not exact.
