cards.title: Current law
cards.body: At any junction, the current flowing in equals the current flowing out. Charge can't pile up or vanish, so the branches must balance.

frames.caption: 40 mA flows in; two of the three ways out carry 15 and 10 mA
In = out: the third wire carries 40 − 15 − 10 = 15 mA

cards.title: Voltage law
cards.body: Go around any closed loop and the voltage rises and drops add to zero. In a single loop, the drops across the parts add up to the source voltage. It is energy bookkeeping: a charge back at its start has gained nothing.

visual.caption: Battery lifts 9 V; R1 drops 3.5 V, R2 the other 5.5 V: sum is 0

cards.title: Current divider
cards.body: When a current splits between two parallel resistors, more goes through the smaller one: I1 = I × R2 / (R1 + R2). By the current law, the other branch carries the rest, I − I1.

visual.caption: I1 = 60 × 200 / 300 = 40 mA through the smaller R1; R2 gets the rest

cards.title: Using them
cards.body: For a tricky network, write a current-law equation at each junction and a voltage-law equation around each loop, then solve them together. The laws hold for any parts, including diodes and transistors.

visual.caption: Kirchhoff's two laws work alongside the two you already know

sources.title: Practical Electronics for Inventors (Scherz & Monk, 2016), ch. 2

cards.title: DC and AC
cards.body: Direct current (DC) flows one way from a steady source like a battery. Alternating current (AC) keeps reversing, usually as a smooth sine wave. Mains is AC, partly because transformers can change AC voltage efficiently.

visual.caption: DC stays on one side of zero; AC swings above and below it

cards.title: Frequency and period
cards.body: Frequency f is the number of full cycles per second, in hertz (Hz). The period T is the time one cycle takes: T = 1 / f and f = 1 / T.
bullets: A 1 µs period means 1 MHz
US mains: 120 V at 60 Hz; much of the world: 220–240 V at 50 Hz

visual.caption: Two full cycles in 2 ms: T = 1 ms, so f = 1 kHz

cards.title: Peak and peak-to-peak
cards.body: The peak (Vp) is the highest point of the wave, measured from 0 V. Peak-to-peak (Vpp) runs from the lowest point to the highest, so for a sine Vpp = 2 × Vp.

visual.caption: From −10 V up to +10 V: Vpp = 20 V

cards.title: RMS values
cards.body: A sine averages to zero, so it is rated by RMS (square, average, square root): the DC voltage that would heat a resistor just as much. Vrms = Vp / √2 ≈ 0.707 × Vp, and Vp ≈ 1.414 × Vrms. Mains ratings like 120 V are RMS.

frames.caption: Equal time above and below zero: a plain average gives 0
Square it: never negative now, and the average is 50
Square root of 50 is 7.07 V: the RMS, at 0.707 of the peak

cards.title: In Python
cards.code:
import math
vrms = 230
vp = vrms * math.sqrt(2)
print(round(vp, 1))      # 325.3
print(round(2 * vp, 1))  # 650.5

visual.caption: The code below works out the 230 V row

cards.title: AC power in resistors
cards.body: With RMS values, Ohm's law and the power formulas work on a plain resistor just as for DC: Irms = Vrms / R, and P = Vrms² / R gives the average power.

visual.caption: Using the peak voltage doubles the answer

sources.title: Practical Electronics for Inventors (Scherz & Monk, 2016), ch. 2

cards.title: Wire gauge
cards.body: Wire thickness is given as a gauge number (AWG in the US). The scale runs backwards: a smaller number means a thicker wire. Thicker wire has less resistance and carries more current; an overloaded thin wire heats up and can melt.

visual.caption: Diameter in mm for each AWG number: bigger number, thinner wire

cards.title: Solid or stranded
cards.body: Magnet wire is a third kind: varnish-coated, for winding coils.

cards.title: Poles and throws
cards.body: A pole is one separate circuit the switch controls; a throw is each contact a pole can connect to. S means single (1) and D means double (2).

visual.caption: A DPDT works two circuits at once, each choosing between two contacts

cards.title: Throwing a switch
cards.body: An SPDT switch has one pole (the common contact) and two throws. Flipping it moves the connection from one throw to the other.

frames.caption: Lever up: common connects to throw A; B is disconnected
Lever down: common connects to throw B instead

cards.title: Push buttons
cards.body: Momentary switches spring back when you let go. Some toggle switches also have a center-off position.

visual.caption: NO connects only while pressed; NC breaks only while pressed

cards.title: Special switches
bullets: Reed switch: two thin contacts in glass that close near a magnet (door alarms)
DIP switch: a row of tiny switches that fits a chip socket
Rotary switch: one pole, many throws, e.g. SP8T

visual.caption: Three switches for special jobs

sources.title: Practical Electronics for Inventors (Scherz & Monk, 2016), ch. 3

cards.title: What a relay is
cards.body: A relay is a switch worked by electricity. A small, low-voltage control circuit can switch a separate, bigger circuit, and the two stay electrically apart.

frames.caption: A low-voltage control circuit drives the coil
Current in a coil makes a magnetic field
The contact is spring-loaded and moves over
The big circuit never touches the control circuit

steps: Coil off: spring pulls it back
frames.caption: With no magnet, the contact returns

cards.title: Kinds of relay
bullets: Contacts are named like switches: SPDT, NO, NC
Coils are rated for a voltage, such as 5, 12 or 24 V DC

visual.caption: Fewer moving parts, faster switching

cards.title: The flyback diode
cards.body: A relay coil is an inductor and fights any sudden change in current. Switch it off and it can kick out a spike of hundreds of volts, enough to destroy the transistor driving it. A diode across the coil gives it a safe loop.

frames.caption: Transistor switch on: current runs through the coil; the diode blocks
Switch off: the coil's current loops through the diode and dies away

cards.title: Fuses and breakers
cards.body: Both protect wiring and parts from shorts and overloads by opening the circuit when the current goes past a rating.

cards.title: Choosing a fuse
bullets: Fast-blow: opens on a brief surge; for sensitive electronics
Slow-blow (time-lag): rides out turn-on surges from motors
On mains, put it in the hot (live) wire, before the device, so a blown fuse cuts off the live voltage

visual.caption: Multiply the normal current by 1.5

sources.title: Practical Electronics for Inventors (Scherz & Monk, 2016), ch. 3

cards.title: Color digits
cards.body: Small through-hole resistors are marked with colored bands. Each color stands for a digit.

visual.caption: Ten colors for the digits 0 to 9

cards.title: Reading four bands
cards.body: Start from the end away from the gold or silver band. Bands 1 and 2 are digits, band 3 is the multiplier (how many zeros to add, a power of ten), and band 4 is the tolerance.

frames.caption: Hold it with the gold band on the right, then read from the left
Band 1 is a digit: green = 5
Band 2 is a digit: blue = 6, so 56 so far
Band 3 is the multiplier: red = 2 zeros, × 100
Band 4 is the tolerance: gold = ±5%

cards.title: Tolerance bands
cards.body: Gold or silver can also appear as band 3: there they multiply by 0.1 or 0.01.

visual.caption: Brown and red mark precision parts

cards.title: Five bands
cards.body: Precision resistors often carry five bands: three digits, then the multiplier, then the tolerance.

frames.caption: Five bands: the first three are digits: 1, 5, 0
Band 4 is the multiplier: red = × 100
Band 5 is the tolerance: brown = ±1%

cards.title: What tolerance means
cards.body: Tolerance is how far the real value may be from the printed one. 5% of 470 Ω is 23.5 Ω either way. For most hobby circuits ±5% is fine.

visual.caption: Take the percentage of the printed value, then go below and above

cards.title: In Python
cards.body: C.index(color) is the color's digit. The lookup scans a fixed list of ten colors: O(1) time and space.
cards.code:
C = ["black", "brown", "red",
     "orange", "yellow", "green",
     "blue", "violet", "gray",
     "white"]

def ohms(b1, b2, b3):
    i = C.index
    n = 10 * i(b1) + i(b2)
    return n * 10 ** i(b3)

print(ohms("green", "blue", "red"))
# 5600

sources.title: Practical Electronics for Inventors (Scherz & Monk, 2016), ch. 3

cards.title: Storing charge
cards.body: A capacitor is two conducting plates with an insulator between them. Put a voltage across it and it stores charge: Q = C × V. Capacitance C is in farads (F); real parts run from a few pF to tens of thousands of µF.

visual.caption: More capacitance or more voltage means more stored charge

cards.title: DC blocked, AC passed
cards.body: Once charged, a capacitor lets no steady DC through. Changing signals pass more easily at higher frequency: reactance Xc = 1 / (2πfC) ohms. In series it blocks DC between stages; from supply to ground it drains noise.

visual.caption: About 3.2 kΩ at 50 Hz, only 159 Ω at 1 kHz: higher f, less opposition

cards.title: Combining capacitors
cards.body: The rules are the opposite of the resistor rules. A parallel group is limited by its lowest voltage rating.

visual.caption: Parallel adds; series (1/C = 1/C1 + 1/C2) is smaller than either

cards.title: RC time constant
cards.body: Charging through a resistor takes time. The time constant is τ = R × C (ohms × farads = seconds): 10 kΩ × 100 µF = 1 s. Charging from 0 V: V = Vs × (1 − e^(−t/τ)). Discharging: V = V0 × e^(−t/τ).

visual.caption: At one τ, charging reaches 63.2% and discharging has fallen to 36.8%

cards.title: Tau by tau
cards.body: Each time constant closes 63.2% of the remaining gap, so the voltage is about full after five.
cards.code:
import math
for n in range(1, 6):
    pct = 100 * (1 - math.exp(-n))
    print(n, round(pct, 1))
# 63.2 86.5 95.0 98.2 99.3

frames.caption: After 1 time constant: 63.2% of the supply
After 2 time constants: 86.5% of the supply
After 3 time constants: 95.0% of the supply
After 4 time constants: 98.2% of the supply
After 5 time constants: 99.3% of the supply (about full)

cards.title: Electrolytics have polarity
cards.body: Reverse an electrolytic, or go past its voltage rating, and it can overheat, leak or burst.

left.title: Electrolytic
points: Large values in a small can

sources.title: Practical Electronics for Inventors (Scherz & Monk, 2016), ch. 3

cards.title: What an inductor is
cards.body: An inductor is a coil of wire, often on an iron or ferrite core. It resists any change in its current: the faster the change, the bigger the voltage it develops (V = L × ΔI / Δt). Inductance L is in henrys (H).

visual.caption: Same 1 A change, done faster: a far bigger voltage

cards.title: AC versus DC
cards.body: Steady DC passes, meeting only the wire's small resistance. AC is opposed more as frequency rises: XL = 2πfL ohms. That is the opposite of a capacitor, and why coils work as chokes against high-frequency noise.

visual.caption: The coil's reactance climbs in step with frequency; the capacitor's falls

cards.title: Combining coils
cards.body: Inductors combine like resistors, as long as the coils don't share magnetic field. Cutting a coil's current suddenly causes a voltage spike.

visual.caption: Series adds; parallel (1/L = 1/L1 + 1/L2) is smaller than either

cards.title: How transformers work
cards.body: A transformer is two coils on one iron core. Steady DC makes no changing field, so a transformer can't convert it.

steps: AC flows in the primary coil
visual.caption: The turns ratio sets the voltage ratio

cards.title: Turns ratio
cards.body: Vs = Vp × Ns / Np. Fewer turns on the secondary steps the voltage down; more turns steps it up.

visual.caption: Row 3 has more secondary turns, so it steps up

cards.title: Current trades off
cards.body: An ideal transformer passes on all its power, so Vp × Ip = Vs × Is. Step the voltage down and the current steps up by the same ratio: Is / Ip = Np / Ns. Real ones waste some power as heat.

visual.caption: Voltage down 20 times, current up 20 times, same power

sources.title: Practical Electronics for Inventors (Scherz & Monk, 2016), ch. 3

cards.title: A one-way valve
cards.body: A diode lets current through in one direction only. It has an anode (the p side) and a cathode (the n side, marked with a band).

cards.title: Forward voltage
bullets: Silicon: about 0.6–0.7 V before it conducts
Schottky: about 0.4 V, and faster
Germanium: about 0.2–0.3 V
Diodes in series add their drops
Limits: max forward current and peak reverse voltage (PIV)

visual.caption: Almost no current until about 0.6 V, then it shoots up

cards.title: AC to DC
cards.body: A rectifier turns AC into DC. One diode (half-wave) passes only the positive halves. A bridge of four diodes uses both halves, but the current always crosses two diodes. A capacitor after it smooths the ripple.

frames.caption: One cycle of AC in (6 V RMS): half above zero, half below
One diode: only the positive half gets through, one drop lower
Bridge: both halves come out positive, two drops below the peak

cards.title: Bridge example
cards.body: The output peak of a bridge is two diode drops below the input peak.

visual.caption: Start from the peak, not the RMS value

cards.title: Other diode jobs
bullets: Series diode: blocks a battery put in backwards
Flyback diode: soaks up a coil's switch-off spike
Zener diode: conducts in reverse at a set voltage, for simple regulators

visual.caption: Three more uses for the one-way valve

sources.title: Practical Electronics for Inventors (Scherz & Monk, 2016), ch. 4

cards.title: Light from a diode
cards.body: An LED is a diode built to give off light when forward-biased. Like any diode it conducts one way only. Brightness follows the current.

cards.title: Forward voltage
cards.body: Typical current is 10–30 mA; assume 20 mA if unsure.

visual.caption: White and blue need the most voltage

cards.title: The series resistor
cards.body: An LED hardly limits its own current: a little above its forward voltage the current shoots up and burns it out. So add a resistor in series: R = (Vsupply − Vled) / I, then round up to the next standard value.
cards.code:
12 V supply, LED drops 3.4 V
want 20 mA
R = (12 - 3.4) / 0.02
  = 430 Ω

visual.caption: The resistor takes the spare 12 − 3.4 = 8.6 V at 20 mA

cards.title: Several LEDs
cards.body: LEDs in series can share one resistor: subtract all their forward voltages from the supply first. Don't run LEDs in parallel from a single resistor; whichever warms up takes more of the current.

frames.caption: Series: R = (12 − 2 − 2) / 0.02 = 400 Ω, one resistor for both
Parallel: give each LED its own resistor, (5 − 2) / 0.02 = 150 Ω

sources.title: Practical Electronics for Inventors (Scherz & Monk, 2016), ch. 5

cards.title: Small controls big
cards.body: A transistor uses a small signal on one lead to control a larger current through the other two, like a hand on a tap. The two big families are bipolar transistors (BJTs) and field-effect transistors (FETs).

left.title: As a switch
points: Turns a load on and off

cards.title: NPN basics
cards.body: An NPN bipolar transistor has a base (B), a collector (C) and an emitter (E). It turns on when current flows into the base, which sits about 0.6–0.7 V above the emitter. A PNP works the same with every polarity flipped.

visual.caption: A small current into the base lets a big one flow from C to E

cards.title: Current gain
cards.body: In its active region a small base current controls a bigger collector current: Ic = β × Ib. The gain β (also written hFE) varies by part, typically 10 to 500. Both currents leave through the emitter: Ie = Ib + Ic.

visual.caption: The collector current is β times the base current

cards.title: Three regions
cards.body: Cutoff and saturation make a switch; the active region makes an amplifier.

visual.caption: In the active region small changes come out bigger

cards.title: As a switch
cards.body: To switch a load, find the base current it needs, Ib = Ic / β, and size the base resistor from the control voltage: Rb = (Vin − 0.7) / Ib. Pick a somewhat smaller resistor so it is surely saturated.

frames.caption: Vin 0 V: no base current, so cutoff. No collector current: load off
Vin 5 V: about 2.4 mA into the base saturates it; 200 mA flows

cards.title: Field-effect transistors (MOSFETs)
cards.body: A common n-channel enhancement MOSFET is off with 0 V on its gate and turns on once the gate is a few volts above the source. FETs are the workhorse of modern chips.

right.title: MOSFET
points: On: gate a few V above source

sources.title: Practical Electronics for Inventors (Scherz & Monk, 2016), ch. 4

cards.title: Two kinds of signal
cards.body: An analog signal can take any value in a range, like a thermometer voltage drifting from 0.31 V to 0.47 V. A digital signal uses just two levels, HIGH and LOW, so each wire carries one bit.

visual.caption: The smooth line takes any value; the square one only two

cards.title: Why go digital
cards.body: Two clean levels are easy to tell apart, so digital circuits can store bits and make logical decisions, which plain analog circuits can't.

cards.title: Logic levels
bullets: Negative true logic swaps them: LOW means true
Each logic family sets its own valid voltage bands; a voltage between them is not a valid level

visual.caption: Positive true logic: HIGH = 1 = true

cards.title: The clock
cards.body: A clock signal flips between HIGH and LOW over and over, f times per second. One full cycle takes T = 1/f seconds, and circuits do their work when it switches.

visual.caption: One full cycle (HIGH then LOW) takes 20 ns

cards.title: Serial or parallel
cards.body: Serial sends a word down one wire, one bit per clock period: n bits take n periods, O(n) time. Parallel gives every bit its own wire and moves the word in one period, but needs n wires.
cards.code:
12-bit word, T = 100 ns
serial:   12 x 100 = 1200 ns
parallel:  1 x 100 =  100 ns

frames.caption: Period 1: bit 1 is on the wire
Period 2: bit 0 is on the wire
Period 3: bit 1 is on the wire
Period 4: bit 1 is on the wire
Serial took 4 periods. Parallel: 4 wires, 1 period

cards.title: Logic families
bullets: Fanout: how many same-family inputs one output can drive
Propagation delay: time from an input change to the output change, in nanoseconds

visual.caption: Two families of logic chips

sources.title: Practical Electronics for Inventors (Scherz & Monk, 2016), ch. 12

cards.title: Place values
cards.body: Binary uses only 0 and 1. Each place is worth twice the place on its right. The leftmost bit is the most significant (MSB), the rightmost the least (LSB). Add the values under every 1.

cards.title: Decimal to binary
cards.body: Divide by 2 again and again and keep each remainder. The first remainder is the LSB and the last one is the MSB, so the bits fill in from the right.

frames.caption: 37 / 2 = 18 remainder 1 (LSB)
18 / 2 = 9 remainder 0
9 / 2 = 4 remainder 1
4 / 2 = 2 remainder 0
2 / 2 = 1 remainder 0
1 / 2 = 0 remainder 1 (MSB)
Quotient is 0, so stop: 37 = 100101

cards.title: In Python
cards.body: divmod(n, 2) gives the whole quotient n // 2 and the remainder n % 2. One loop pass per bit: O(log n) time, and O(log n) space for the digits.

cards.title: Hexadecimal (base 16)
cards.body: Hex is base 16: digits 0 to 9, then A to F for 10 to 15. One hex digit is exactly 4 bits.

cards.title: Binary to hex
cards.body: Split the bits into groups of 4 from the right (pad with 0s on the left) and swap each group for its digit. Octal does the same with groups of 3. Going back: 0x3A = 0011 1010 = 58.

frames.caption: Split into groups of 4 bits, starting from the right

cards.title: Handy facts
bullets: Decimal to hex: divide by 16 and keep the remainders, like with 2
Python: hex(235) gives '0xeb', int('EB', 16) gives 235

visual.caption: Every 4 bits make one hex digit

sources.title: Practical Electronics for Inventors (Scherz & Monk, 2016), ch. 12

cards.title: Binary-coded decimal
cards.body: BCD stores each decimal digit in its own 4-bit group. It suits digit displays like clocks and meters. Only 0000 to 1001 (0 to 9) are valid groups; 1010 to 1111 never appear.

visual.caption: Each digit of 407 gets its own 4 bits

cards.title: BCD is not binary
cards.body: Converting digit by digit is not the same as converting the whole number. BCD needs more bits for the same value: 407 is 12 bits in BCD but 9 bits (1 1001 0111) in binary.

visual.caption: Same number, different bit patterns

cards.title: Two's complement
cards.body: Circuits store negatives in two's complement. Positives are plain binary. For a negative, write the positive value, flip every bit (the one's complement), then add 1.

frames.caption: Flip every bit: the one's complement
Add 1: 1111 0111 is -9. The top bit 1 means negative

cards.title: Reading the sign
cards.body: The top bit shows the sign: 1 means negative. 8 bits hold -128 to +127. Sign-magnitude, which only sets the top bit (-9 would be 1000 1001), is rarely used for math.

visual.caption: Every pattern starting with 1 is negative

cards.title: Adding in binary
cards.body: Add columns from the right: 0+1 = 1, 1+1 = 10 (write 0, carry 1), 1+1+1 = 11 (write 1, carry 1). n-bit numbers take n column steps: O(n).

frames.caption: Column 1: 0+1 = 1: write 1, no carry
Column 2: 1+1 = 10: write 0, carry 1
Column 4: 1+0+1 = 10: write 0, carry 1
Column 8: 0+0+1 = 1: write 1, no carry

cards.title: Subtract by adding
cards.body: With two's complement, subtracting is adding the negative; drop any carry out of the top bit. Python's & 0xFF keeps the low 8 bits.

sources.title: Practical Electronics for Inventors (Scherz & Monk, 2016), ch. 12

cards.title: What a gate does
cards.body: A logic gate takes one or more input bits and gives one output bit. A truth table lists the output for every input combination. n inputs give 2ⁿ rows, so writing out a full table takes O(2ⁿ) time.

visual.caption: Each extra input doubles the rows

cards.title: The basic gates
bullets: NOT: flips its one input
AND: 1 only if every input is 1
OR: 1 if at least one input is 1
XOR: 1 if the two inputs differ

visual.caption: Find the 1s: AND has one, OR three, XOR the two mixed rows

cards.title: Flipped outputs
cards.body: NAND, NOR and XNOR are AND, OR and XOR with the output flipped. Step through and compare each pair of columns.

frames.caption: NOT has one input and flips it
NAND is 0 only when every input is 1
NOR is 1 only when every input is 0
XNOR is 1 when the two inputs are equal

cards.title: More inputs
cards.body: AND, OR, NAND and NOR also come with 3, 4 or 8 inputs. A 4-input AND gives 1 in only one of its 16 rows (all 1s), and a 4-input OR gives 0 in only one row (all 0s). NAND and NOR flip those, so their counts swap.

visual.caption: 16 rows each: flipping the output swaps the counts

cards.title: Gates in Python
cards.body: On the bits 0 and 1, Python's & is AND, | is OR and ^ is XOR. 1 - x flips a bit.
cards.code:
a, b = 1, 0
print(a & b)        # AND  0
print(a | b)        # OR   1
print(a ^ b)        # XOR  1
print(1 - a)        # NOT  0
print(1 - (a & b))  # NAND 1
print(int(a == b))  # XNOR 0

sources.title: Practical Electronics for Inventors (Scherz & Monk, 2016), ch. 12

visual.caption: + is OR, so 1 + 1 = 1. Books draw A' as a bar over A

cards.title: Handy identities
cards.body: Each OR rule has an AND twin. Two more worth knowing: A + A·B = A (absorption) and A·(B + C) = A·B + A·C.

visual.caption: Row 4: a thing OR its opposite is 1; AND its opposite is 0

cards.title: Simplifying an expression
cards.body: Fewer terms mean fewer gates. Factor out what the terms share, then apply the identities.

frames.caption: Y' appears in both terms
Factor out the shared Y'
X + X' = 1: a thing OR its opposite
1·Y' = Y': the output ignores X

cards.title: De Morgan's laws
cards.body: To split a bar over a group, flip each variable and swap AND with OR. So a NAND acts like an OR with inverted inputs, and a NOR like an AND with inverted inputs. This is called bubble pushing.

frames.caption: NAND = OR of the inverted inputs: the columns match
NOR = AND of the inverted inputs: the columns match

cards.title: Check every row
cards.body: Two expressions are equal if they agree on every row. With n variables that is 2ⁿ rows: O(2ⁿ) time.
cards.code:
rows = [(0,0), (0,1), (1,0), (1,1)]
for a, b in rows:
    assert 1-(a|b) == (1-a)&(1-b)
print('De Morgan holds')

cards.title: Universal gates
cards.body: NAND alone can build every other gate, and so can NOR. Simplified designs usually end up as a sum of products (ORed AND terms, like A·B + C) or a product of sums; Karnaugh maps help find the simplest.

frames.caption: Tie a NAND's inputs together and it becomes NOT
Put that NOT after a NAND and you get AND

sources.title: Practical Electronics for Inventors (Scherz & Monk, 2016), ch. 12

cards.title: No memory
cards.body: In combinational logic the output depends only on the inputs right now. Common blocks come ready-made as chips.

visual.caption: Nothing is stored: same inputs, same output, every time

cards.title: Mux and demux
cards.body: A multiplexer (mux) uses n select lines to choose one of 2ⁿ inputs and pass it to its one output. A demultiplexer does the reverse: it sends one input to one of 2ⁿ outputs.

frames.caption: Select 00 passes D0 to the output Y
Select 01 passes D1 to the output Y
Select 10 passes D2 to the output Y
Select 11 passes D3 to the output Y

cards.title: Decoder and encoder
cards.body: A decoder turns an n-bit code into exactly one active line out of 2ⁿ. An encoder is the reverse: the one active input becomes its binary code. A priority encoder picks the highest if several are active.

visual.caption: 2-to-4 decoder: each code turns on one line (H)

cards.title: Active-low outputs
cards.body: Many decoders mark the chosen line by pulling it LOW while every other line stays HIGH. A bubble on the pin, or a bar over its name, shows this.

visual.caption: Active-low: code 10 makes only Y2 LOW

cards.title: Half and full adders
cards.body: A half adder adds two bits: sum = A XOR B, carry = A AND B. A full adder also takes a carry in: two half adders (A with B, then that sum with the carry in) plus an OR that merges their carries.
cards.code:
def half_add(a, b):
    return a ^ b, a & b

print(half_add(1, 1))  # (0, 1)
print(half_add(1, 0))  # (1, 0)

frames.caption: Half adder: 1 + 1 = 10, so sum 0 and carry 1
Full adder: Cout is 1 when two or more inputs are 1

cards.title: Ripple-carry adder
cards.body: Chain n full adders, each carry out feeding the next carry in. The top stage must wait for the carry to ripple through every stage: worst case n stage delays, O(n) time, using O(n) gates. 8 stages at 5 ns: 40 ns.

frames.caption: Stage 1 done after 5 ns: sum 0, carry out 1
Stage 2 done after 10 ns: sum 0, carry out 1
Stage 3 done after 15 ns: sum 0, carry out 1
Stage 4 done after 20 ns: sum 1, carry out 0

sources.title: Practical Electronics for Inventors (Scherz & Monk, 2016), ch. 12

cards.title: Logic with memory
cards.body: Sequential logic stores bits, so its output depends on past inputs as well as present ones. The basic one-bit store is a latch or flip-flop. A clock usually decides when it takes in new data.

cards.title: SR latch
cards.body: Two cross-coupled NOR gates with inputs S (set) and R (reset). S = R = 1 forces both outputs to 0, and the state after release is a race, so it is avoided. A NAND latch has active-low inputs: its hold state is 1 1.

visual.caption: With S = R = 0 the latch keeps whatever it stored

cards.title: Level vs edge
cards.body: A level-triggered (gated) latch follows its inputs the whole time its clock or enable is HIGH. An edge-triggered flip-flop looks only at the instant the clock rises (or falls) and ignores changes at any other time.

visual.caption: D rises while the clock is HIGH: the latch follows, the flip-flop waits

cards.title: D flip-flop
cards.body: A D flip-flop feeds D to S and an inverted copy to R, so S = R = 1 can't happen. At each active clock edge Q takes the value of D; between edges Q holds. D must be steady for a short setup time before the edge.

frames.caption: Edge 1: Q copies D = 1, so Q goes 0 to 1
Edge 2: Q copies D = 1 (no change)
Edge 3: Q copies D = 0, so Q goes 1 to 0
Edge 4: Q copies D = 1, so Q goes 0 to 1

cards.title: JK flip-flop
cards.body: JK works like SR, but J = K = 1 toggles instead of being forbidden: Q flips on every active edge.

visual.caption: Only the last row differs from the SR latch

cards.title: Tracing a JK
cards.body: Q starts at 1. Apply one row of the JK table at each clock edge.

frames.caption: Edge 1: J K = 0 1 is reset, so Q goes 1 to 0
Edge 2: J K = 1 1 is toggle, so Q goes 0 to 1
Edge 3: J K = 0 0 is hold, so Q goes 1 to 1
Edge 4: J K = 1 1 is toggle, so Q goes 1 to 0

sources.title: Practical Electronics for Inventors (Scherz & Monk, 2016), ch. 12

cards.title: Counting with toggles
cards.body: A flip-flop in toggle mode flips once per clock edge, so its output runs at half the clock frequency. Chain n, each clocked by the one before, for a ripple counter: it counts 0 to 2ⁿ - 1 (MOD-2ⁿ) and divides the clock by 2ⁿ.

frames.caption: Count 0
Count 1: Q0 flips on every clock edge
Count 2
Count 3
Count 4
Count 5
Count 6
Count 7: all 1s, the next edge wraps to 0

cards.title: Sizing a counter
cards.body: n flip-flops give 2ⁿ states. Each stage also halves the frequency: 100 kHz into 4 stages comes out at 100 / 16 = 6.25 kHz.

visual.caption: States double with each flip-flop; the top count is states - 1

cards.title: Ripple vs synchronous
cards.body: In a ripple counter delays add up: 4 stages of 25 ns settle 100 ns after the edge, O(n) for n stages. A synchronous counter uses gates to pick which flip-flops toggle.

cards.title: Shift registers
cards.body: A row of D flip-flops where each Q feeds the next D. On each clock edge every bit moves one place, so loading n bits serially takes n clocks.
bullets: Serial-in, serial-out: delays a bit stream
Serial-in, parallel-out: collects bits into a word
Parallel-in, serial-out: sends a word one bit per clock

frames.caption: A 4-bit register, empty. Bits 1, 0, 1 will enter on the left
Clock 1: 1 enters, every bit moves one place right
Clock 2: 0 enters, every bit moves one place right
Clock 3: 1 enters, every bit moves one place right

cards.title: Ring and Johnson
cards.body: Feed the last output back to the first input and a single 1 goes round: a ring counter of n flip-flops has n states (100, 010, 001). Feed back the inverted last output instead for a Johnson counter with 2n states.

frames.caption: Start: all 0s
Clock 1: the inverted last bit (1) enters on the left
Clock 2: the inverted last bit (1) enters on the left
Clock 3: the inverted last bit (1) enters on the left
Clock 4: the inverted last bit (0) enters on the left
Clock 5: the inverted last bit (0) enters on the left
Back to 000 after 6 states (2 x 3)

cards.title: Shifting in Python
cards.body: A list can model a register. Each shift copies the list: O(n) time and space per clock, though hardware moves all bits at once. To shift right instead, use [bit] + reg[:-1].
cards.code:
reg = [0, 0, 0]
for bit in [1, 1, 0]:
    reg = reg[1:] + [bit]  # left
    print(reg)

frames.caption: 1 enters on the right; the others move left: prints [0, 0, 1]
1 enters on the right; the others move left: prints [0, 1, 1]
0 enters on the right; the others move left: prints [1, 1, 0]

sources.title: Practical Electronics for Inventors (Scherz & Monk, 2016), ch. 12

cards.title: Tables and queries
cards.body: A table stores rows, and every row has the same named columns. A SELECT query describes the rows and columns you want; the database works out how to fetch them. Keywords are not case-sensitive, and a statement ends with a semicolon.

visual.caption: The songs table used in every example. NULL marks a missing value

cards.title: Pick and filter
cards.body: SELECT lists the columns (* means all), FROM names the table, and WHERE keeps only rows where the condition is true.
cards.code:
SELECT title, plays
FROM songs
WHERE year >= 2000
  AND plays > 100;

frames.caption: FROM songs: start with every row
year >= 2000 is true for four rows; Tide (1998) fails
AND plays > 100: Echo (60) fails, and Spark's NULL is not true
SELECT keeps just the two columns you asked for

cards.title: AND before OR
cards.body: AND binds tighter than OR, so a OR b AND c is read as a OR (b AND c). Use parentheses when you mix them.

left.title: No parentheses
points: AND goes first: all of artist 1

right.title: With parentheses
points: The year test now hits everyone

visual.caption: Same words, different rows: Glow (2019) only survives on the left

cards.title: Handy filters
bullets: IN: matches any value in the list.
BETWEEN: a range that includes both ends.
LIKE: % stands for any run of characters, _ for exactly one. In SQLite, LIKE ignores case for plain letters.
DISTINCT: drops duplicate rows, so SELECT DISTINCT artist_id gives 1, 2, NULL.

visual.caption: Each filter run on songs. 'd%' still finds Drift: LIKE ignores case here

cards.title: Sorting and limits
cards.body: ORDER BY sorts ascending unless you add DESC; extra columns break ties. LIMIT n keeps the first n rows (SQL Server uses TOP instead). Without ORDER BY, row order is not guaranteed.
cards.code:
SELECT title, year
FROM songs
ORDER BY year DESC
LIMIT 2;

frames.caption: The two columns, in no promised order
ORDER BY year DESC: newest first
LIMIT 2 keeps only the first two rows

cards.title: Clause order, cost
cards.body: Write clauses in this order: SELECT, FROM, WHERE, GROUP BY, HAVING, ORDER BY, LIMIT. With no index, WHERE has to scan every row: O(n) time. ORDER BY needs a sort, O(n log n) time and O(n) space, unless an index already keeps that order.

visual.caption: The order you write the clauses in, top to bottom

cards.title: Unknown, not zero
cards.body: NULL marks a missing or unknown value. It is not 0 and not the empty string ''. Comparing anything with NULL gives NULL (unknown), and so does arithmetic with it.

visual.caption: Even NULL = NULL is unknown. Only IS NULL gives a real answer

cards.title: Test with IS
cards.body: Use IS NULL and IS NOT NULL; = NULL never matches. WHERE keeps only rows where the condition is true, so unknown rows quietly drop out.
cards.code:
SELECT title FROM songs
WHERE plays IS NULL;

frames.caption: WHERE plays IS NULL: one row, Spark
WHERE plays = NULL: no rows at all, the test is never true
WHERE plays IS NOT NULL: the other four

cards.title: Three-valued logic
cards.body: A test can be TRUE, FALSE or NULL. A FALSE settles an AND and a TRUE settles an OR; otherwise the NULL wins. NOT NULL is still NULL.

visual.caption: Read across: only FALSE AND NULL and TRUE OR NULL get a sure answer

cards.title: Rows that vanish
cards.body: WHERE x <> 5 also skips rows where x is NULL, because NULL <> 5 is unknown, not true. Add OR x IS NULL if you want them.

frames.caption: 4 <> 5 is TRUE: the row is kept
NULL <> 5 is NULL, not true: the row is dropped
5 <> 5 is FALSE: dropped. Only one of three rows comes back

cards.title: Filling the gaps
cards.body: COALESCE(a, b, ...) returns its first argument that is not NULL. SQLite also has IFNULL(a, b) for two arguments.

visual.caption: Spark's NULL becomes 0; every other row passes through unchanged

cards.title: Aggregate functions
cards.body: COUNT(*) counts rows. COUNT(col), SUM, AVG, MIN and MAX skip NULLs, so AVG divides by 4 here, not 5.
cards.code:
SELECT COUNT(*),      -- 5
       COUNT(plays),  -- 4
       SUM(plays),    -- 1530
       AVG(plays)     -- 382.5
FROM songs;

visual.caption: The plays column: 5 rows, but the NULL is skipped, so 1530 / 4 = 382.5

cards.title: Grouping rows
cards.body: GROUP BY puts rows with the same value into one group and returns one row per group. Each selected column should be grouped or wrapped in an aggregate; SQLite lets other columns through, but their values come from just one row of the group.

frames.caption: GROUP BY artist_id: start with all five rows
Rows with the same artist_id are put together: the artist 1 group
The artist 2 group. Echo's NULL makes a group of its own
One row per group. SUM skips Spark's NULL, so artist 2 totals 900

cards.title: WHERE versus HAVING
cards.body: WHERE filters rows before grouping. HAVING filters groups after the aggregates exist, so COUNT(*) belongs in HAVING; in WHERE it is an error.
cards.code:
SELECT artist_id,
       COUNT(*) AS n
FROM songs
WHERE year > 2000
GROUP BY artist_id
HAVING COUNT(*) >= 2;
-- artist 1, n = 2

frames.caption: WHERE year > 2000 runs first, on rows: Tide (1998) is out
GROUP BY artist_id counts what is left in each group
HAVING COUNT(*) >= 2 runs last, on groups: only artist 1 stays

cards.title: Run order, cost
cards.body: The database runs FROM, then WHERE, GROUP BY, HAVING, SELECT, ORDER BY and LIMIT. Grouping by sorting costs O(n log n) time; grouping with a hash table costs O(n) average time and O(g) space for g groups.

visual.caption: Run order, not writing order. WHERE comes before the groups, HAVING after

cards.title: Why join
cards.body: Data is split over tables that point at each other with keys: songs.artist_id holds an id from artists. A join puts matching rows side by side, and ON gives the matching rule. Short aliases (FROM songs AS s) keep column names clear: s.title.

frames.caption: songs: each row names its artist by number only
artists: the numbers live here. Nobody points at Quill

cards.title: INNER JOIN
cards.body: Plain JOIN means INNER JOIN: only rows with a match on both sides.
cards.code:
SELECT s.title, a.name
FROM songs AS s
JOIN artists AS a
  ON a.id = s.artist_id;

frames.caption: Glow: artist_id 1 matches Nova, so a row is added
Drift: artist_id 1 matches Nova, so a row is added
Tide: artist_id 2 matches Lumen, so a row is added
Spark: artist_id 2 matches Lumen, so a row is added
Echo: artist_id is NULL, nothing matches, so no row is added

cards.title: LEFT JOIN
cards.body: Every row of the left table stays. Where nothing matches, the right side's columns are NULL.
cards.code:
SELECT a.name, s.title
FROM artists AS a
LEFT JOIN songs AS s
  ON s.artist_id = a.id;

visual.caption: 5 rows: Nova 2, Lumen 2, and Quill kept once with a NULL title

cards.title: Rows with no match
cards.body: After a LEFT JOIN, add WHERE s.id IS NULL to keep only the left rows that matched nothing: artists with no songs.

frames.caption: The LEFT JOIN result: every artist is present
WHERE s.id IS NULL keeps only the row the join had to pad: Quill

cards.title: What joins cost
cards.body: n and m are the row counts of the two tables. A join with no matching rule (CROSS JOIN) returns every pair: 3 artists × 5 songs = 15 rows.

visual.caption: Nested loop: no index compares every pair; an index makes each lookup O(log m)

cards.title: Adding rows
cards.body: List the columns, then VALUES with one value per column. Columns you leave out get their default, or NULL. You can add several rows at once: VALUES (...), (...).

visual.caption: The new row: id filled itself in as 6, and plays, left out, is NULL

cards.title: Changing rows
cards.body: SET gives the new values and WHERE picks the rows. A row whose plays is NULL stays NULL, since NULL + 10 is NULL.

frames.caption: WHERE artist_id = 2 picks two rows: Tide and Spark
Tide goes 900 to 910. Spark stays NULL: NULL + 10 is NULL

cards.title: Removing rows
cards.body: DELETE removes rows but keeps the table; DROP TABLE removes the table itself.
cards.code:
DELETE FROM songs
WHERE year < 2000;

frames.caption: WHERE year < 2000 matches one row: Tide, 1998
Tide is gone. The table and the other four rows remain

cards.title: Mind the WHERE
cards.body: UPDATE or DELETE with no WHERE hits every row. Cost: finding rows is O(n) without an index, and each change also updates every index on the table.

visual.caption: A safe routine: look first, change inside a transaction, then decide

cards.title: Primary keys
cards.body: A primary key is a column, or set of columns, whose value picks out exactly one row. The database rejects a duplicate. In SQLite an INTEGER PRIMARY KEY column fills itself in with the next number when you leave it out of an INSERT.

frames.caption: artists.id is the primary key: no two rows share a value
INSERT INTO artists (name) VALUES ('Vale'): id fills in as 4
INSERT ... VALUES (2, 'Dup') is refused: id 2 is taken

cards.title: Foreign keys
cards.body: A foreign key column holds a key from another table: songs.artist_id points at artists.id. A NULL foreign key is allowed.

visual.caption: Songs (left) point at their artist. Echo's key is NULL, so it points nowhere

cards.title: What the checks refuse
cards.body: With checks on, the database refuses a child row whose parent doesn't exist, and by default refuses to delete a parent that rows still point at.

visual.caption: No artist 99 exists; Nova still has songs; nothing points at Quill

cards.title: Turn checks on
cards.body: SQLite leaves foreign key checks off unless each connection runs PRAGMA foreign_keys = ON (or = 1), outside a transaction. With them off, the bad row below would be saved.
cards.code:
import sqlite3
db = sqlite3.connect(":memory:")
db.execute("PRAGMA foreign_keys=1")
db.executescript("""
CREATE TABLE a(id INTEGER
  PRIMARY KEY);
CREATE TABLE b(a_id INTEGER
  REFERENCES a(id));""")
try:
    db.execute(
        "INSERT INTO b VALUES (99)")
except sqlite3.IntegrityError as e:
    print(e)  # FOREIGN KEY ...

visual.caption: The first three reject a bad row; DEFAULT only supplies a missing value

cards.title: A sorted lookup
cards.body: An index is a separate, sorted copy of one or more columns, with a pointer to each row, like the index at the back of a book. SQLite stores it as a B-tree.
cards.code:
CREATE INDEX idx_songs_year
ON songs(year);

visual.caption: The index on year: years in order, each with the id of its row

cards.title: Why it is faster
cards.body: Without an index, finding rows means a full table scan: O(n). With one, the database searches the tree in O(log n), then fetches the rows. Range filters, joins and ORDER BY on that column can use it too.

frames.caption: 2021 is bigger than 2010: go right, the left half is ruled out
2021 is bigger than 2020: go right, the left half is ruled out
Found 2021 after 3 steps; a scan of 7 rows could take 7

cards.title: Scan versus search
cards.body: An index on (a, b) helps queries on a, or a and b, but usually not on b alone.

visual.caption: At 1,024 rows a scan can take 1,024 steps; the tree takes about 10

cards.title: See the plan
cards.body: Put EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN in front of a query to see how SQLite will run it.

visual.caption: Left: the plan before CREATE INDEX. Right: the plan after

cards.title: What it costs
bullets: UNIQUE and primary key columns are indexed for you (an INTEGER PRIMARY KEY is the table's own sort key).
A plain index allows duplicates; only UNIQUE refuses them.
Index columns you often search, join or sort on, not every column.

right.title: You pay
points: Each INSERT and DELETE, and each
UPDATE of an indexed column, also
updates the index: O(log n) each

visual.caption: Reads get faster, writes get slower

cards.title: Each fact once
cards.body: Normalizing means splitting tables so each fact is stored in one place. Here Ana's town is copied into every order she makes.

visual.caption: The orders table: 'Ana lives in Leeds' is stored twice

cards.title: Three anomalies
bullets: Update: Ana moves, you fix one row and miss the other.
Insert: you can't record a new customer until they order.
Delete: removing Ben's only order also loses his town.

frames.caption: Update: order 1 now says Hull, order 2 still says Leeds. Which is right?
Insert: new customer Cy has no order yet, so no id and no item to store
Delete: Ben's only order is removed, and his town York goes with it

cards.title: The first three forms
bullets: 1NF: each cell holds a single value (no 'pen,ink' lists), and a key identifies each row.
2NF: 1NF, and every non-key column depends on the whole key, not part of a two-column key.
3NF: 2NF, and no non-key column depends on another non-key column.

frames.caption: Breaks 1NF: one cell holds a list of two items
1NF: one value per cell, one row per item
Breaks 3NF: town depends on name, and neither is the key (id)

cards.title: The fix
cards.body: Split the example into customers(id, name, town) and orders(id, customer_id, item). Now the town lives in one row.

frames.caption: customers: each town is stored once
orders: just a customer_id pointing at the customers table

cards.title: The trade-off
cards.body: The price is more joins when you read; some systems copy data back on purpose (denormalize) to make reads faster.

visual.caption: Normalize for safe changes; denormalize only when reads must be faster
